entries.title: Suez Canal
entries.summary: The Suez Canal opened on 17 November 1869, connecting the Mediterranean and Red seas across Egypt. Ships travelling between Europe and Asia could use the new waterway instead of making the much longer passage around southern Africa.
body:
The Suez Canal opened on 17 November 1869 after ten years of construction. It crossed Egypt’s isthmus at sea level, connecting the Mediterranean and Red seas and creating a direct shipping route between the North Atlantic and northern Indian Ocean.

Ships could avoid the much longer journey around southern Africa, changing trade routes between Europe and Asia. Ferdinand de Lesseps had founded the Compagnie de Suez in 1858 to build the canal, which runs from Port Said in the north to Suez in the south.
story_headings: A sea-level route between the Mediterranean and Red seas

provenance.date_note: Suez Canal formally opens17November1869.
provenance.full_source_extract:
The Suez Canal (; Egyptian Arabic: قناة السويس, Qanāt as-Suwais) is an artificial sea-level waterway in Egypt, connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea through the Isthmus of Suez and dividing Africa and Asia (and by extension, the Sinai Peninsula from the rest of Egypt). The 193.3-kilometre-long (120.1-mile) canal is a key trade route between Europe and Asia.
In 1858, French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps formed the Compagnie de Suez for the express purpose of building the canal. Construction of the canal lasted from 1859 to 1869 and it officially opened on 17 November 1869. It offers vessels a direct route between the North Atlantic and northern Indian oceans via the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea, avoiding the South Atlantic and southern Indian oceans and reducing the journey distance from the Arabian Sea to London by approximately 8,900 km (5,500 mi), to 10 days at 20 knots (37 km/h; 23 mph) or 8 days at 24 knots (44 km/h; 28 mph). The canal extends from the northern terminus of Port Said to the southern terminus of Port Tewfik at the city of Suez. In 2021, more than 20,600 vessels traversed the canal (an average of 56 per day).
The original canal featured a single-lane waterway with passing locations in the Ballah Bypass and the Great Bitter Lake. It contained, according to Alois Negrelli's plans, no locks, with seawater flowing freely through it. In general, the water in the canal north of the Bitter Lakes flows north in winter and south in summer. South of the lakes, the current changes with the tide at Suez.
The canal was the property of the Egyptian government, but European shareholders, mostly British and French, owned the concessionary company which operated it until July 1956, when President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised it—an event which led to the Suez Crisis of October–November 1956. The canal is operated and maintained by the state-owned Suez Canal Authority of Egypt. Under the Convention of Constantinople, it may be used "in time of war as in time of peace, by every vessel of commerce or of war, without distinction of flag." Nevertheless, the canal has played an important military strategic role as a naval short-cut and choke point. Navies with coastlines and bases on both the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea (Egypt and Israel) have a particular interest in the Suez Canal. After Egypt closed the Suez Canal at the beginning of the Six-Day War on 5 June 1967, the canal remained closed for eight years, reopening on 5 June 1975.
The Egyptian government launched construction in 2014 to expand and widen the Ballah Bypass for 35 km (22 mi) to speed up the canal's transit time. The expansion was intended to nearly double the capacity of the Suez Canal, from 49 to 97 ships per day. At a cost of LE (Egyptian Pound) 59.4 billion (US$9 billion), this project was funded with interest-bearing investment certificates issued exclusively to Egyptian entities and individuals.
The Suez Canal Authority officially opened the new side channel in 2016. This side channel, at the northern side of the east extension of the Suez Canal, serves the East Terminal for berthing and unberthing vessels from the terminal. As the East Container Terminal is located on the Canal itself, before the construction of the new side channel, it was not possible to berth or unberth vessels at the terminal while a convoy was running.

entries.title: Henri Matisse
entries.summary: Henri Matisse was a French artist born in Le Cateau-Cambrésis on 31 December 1869.
body: Henri Matisse was a French artist born in Le Cateau-Cambrésis on 31 December 1869. His paintings use colour as a structural element rather than simply a description of an object’s surface. In the early twentieth century he became associated with Fauvism, whose bright, non-naturalistic colours challenged expectations of pictorial realism. His subjects included people, interiors and landscapes, while drawing and sculpture offered other ways to simplify a figure and organise the relationship between forms.

In his later years, Matisse developed cut-outs made from paper painted with gouache. Assistants prepared the sheets and helped arrange pieces that he cut and repositioned. The Snail, completed in 1953, places large coloured shapes in a loose spiral, suggesting its subject without outlining a literal shell. The work brings drawing and colour together through the act of cutting. Its apparently simple arrangement depends on the balance of neighbouring colours, uneven edges and areas of exposed white paper.

entries.title: Unification of Germany
entries.summary: German unification brought the German states into a federal empire under Prussian leadership. The proclamation of 18 January 1871 became its symbolic founding moment, within a longer process of alliances, constitutional change and diplomatic settlement.
body:
German unification created a federal empire led by Prussia. The North German Confederation Treaty of 18 August 1866 had established an alliance dominated by the Prussian kingdom; a subsequent constitution strengthened that union. Southern German states joined in 1871.

The ceremonial proclamation of the German Empire on 18 January 1871 became its symbolic founding moment. Constitutional changes and the Treaty of Frankfurt completed the legal and diplomatic process later that year.
story_headings: A Prussian-led federation becomes an empire

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Unification of Germany (German: Deutsche Einigung, pronounced [ˈdɔʏtʃə ˈʔaɪnɪɡʊŋ] ) was a process of building the first nation-state for Germans with federal features based on the concept of Lesser Germany (one without the Habsburgs' multi-ethnic Austria or its German-speaking part). It commenced on 18 August 1866 with the adoption of the North German Confederation Treaty establishing the North German Confederation, initially a military alliance de facto dominated by the Kingdom of Prussia, which was subsequently deepened through adoption of the North German Constitution.
The process symbolically concluded when the south German states joined the North German Confederation with the ceremonial proclamation of the German Empire (German Reich) having 25 member states and led by the Kingdom of Prussia of Hohenzollerns on 18 January 1871; the event was typically celebrated as the date of the German Empire's foundation, although the legally meaningful events relevant to the completion of unification occurred on 1 January 1871 (accession of South German states and constitutional adoption of the name "German Empire"), 4 May 1871 (entry into force of the permanent Constitution of the German Empire), and 10 May 1871 (Treaty of Frankfurt and recognition of the Empire by the French Third Republic).
Despite the legal, administrative, and political disruption caused by the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, the German-speaking people of the old Empire had a common linguistic, cultural, and legal tradition. European liberalism offered an intellectual basis for unification by challenging dynastic and absolutist models of social and political organization; its German manifestation emphasized the importance of tradition, education, and linguistic unity. Economically, the creation of the Prussian Zollverein (customs union) in 1818, and its subsequent expansion to include other states of the Austrian Empire-led German Confederation, increased economic integration between and within states. Emerging modes of transportation facilitated business and recreational travel, leading to contact and sometimes conflict between and among German-speakers from throughout Central Europe. The model of diplomatic spheres of influence resulting from the Congress of Vienna in 1814–1815 after the Napoleonic Wars endorsed Austrian dominance in Central Europe through Habsburg leadership of the German Confederation, designed to replace the Holy Roman Empire. The negotiators at Vienna underestimated Prussia's growing internal strength and declined to create a second coalition of the German states under Prussia's influence, and so failed to foresee that Prussia (Kingdom of Prussia) would rise to challenge Austria for leadership of the German peoples. This German dualism presented two solutions to the problem of unification: Kleindeutsche Lösung, the small Germany solution (Germany without Austria), or Großdeutsche Lösung, the greater Germany solution (Germany with Austria or its German-speaking part), ultimately settled in favor of the former solution in the Peace of Prague.
Historians debate whether Otto von Bismarck—Minister President of Prussia—had a master plan to expand the North German Confederation of 1866 to include the remaining independent German states into a single entity or simply that he planned to expand the power of the Kingdom of Prussia. They conclude that factors other than the strength of Bismarck's Realpolitik led a collection of early modern polities to reorganize their political, economic, military, and diplomatic relationships in the 19th century. Reaction to Danish and French nationalism prompted expressions of German unity. Military successes—especially those of Prussia—in three regional wars generated enthusiasm and pride that politicians could harness to promote unification. This experience echoed the memory of mutual accomplishment in the Napoleonic Wars, particularly in the War of Liberation of 1813–1814. By establishing a Germany without multi-ethnic Austria (under Austria-Hungary) or its German-speaking part, the political and administrative unification of 1871 avoided, at least temporarily,  the problem of dualism.
Despite undergoing in later years several further changes of its name and borders, overhauls of its constitutional system, periods of limited sovereignty and interrupted unity of its territory or government, and despite dissolution of its dominant founding federated state, the polity resulting from the unification process continues today, surviving as the Federal Republic of Germany.

entries.title: Yellowstone National Park
entries.summary: Yellowstone, established on 1 March 1872, was the United States’ first national park and is widely regarded as the world’s first. Its wildlife, geothermal activity and forests occupy a region inhabited by Native Americans for thousands of years.
body:
Yellowstone National Park lies mainly in northwestern Wyoming, with smaller areas in Montana and Idaho. Wildlife and geothermal features, including the popular Old Faithful geyser, make it especially well known. Its landscapes encompass several biomes, most extensively subalpine forest, and belong to the South Central Rockies forests ecoregion.

Native Americans have lived in the Yellowstone region for at least 11,000 years. Non-Native mountain men visited during the early and middle nineteenth century, while organised exploration by non-Natives began in the late 1860s.

The 42nd US Congress established the park through the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act, which President Ulysses S. Grant signed on 1 March 1872. It was the first national park in the United States and is widely regarded as the first in the world.
story_headings: A national park in a long-inhabited landscape

provenance.date_note: Yellowstone established1March1872.
provenance.full_source_extract:
Yellowstone National Park is a national park of the United States located mainly in the northwest corner of the state of Wyoming, with small portions extending into Montana and Idaho. The park is known for its wildlife and its many geothermal features, especially the Old Faithful geyser, one of its most popular. While it represents many types of biomes, subalpine forest is the most abundant. It is part of the South Central Rockies forests ecoregion.
Native Americans have lived in the Yellowstone region for at least 11,000 years. While non-native mountain men visited during the early-to-mid-19th century, organized exploration by non-natives did not begin until the late 1860s. The park was established by the 42nd U.S. Congress through the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act and signed into law by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872. Yellowstone was the first national park in the US, and is also widely understood to be the first national park in the world.
Management and control of the park originally fell under the jurisdiction of the U.S. Department of the Interior, the first Secretary of the Interior to supervise the park being Columbus Delano. However, the U.S. Army was eventually commissioned to oversee the management of Yellowstone for 30 years between 1886 and 1916. In 1917, the administration of the park was transferred to the National Park Service, which had been created the previous year. Hundreds of structures have been built and are protected for their architectural and historical significance, and researchers have examined more than one thousand indigenous archaeological sites.
Yellowstone National Park spans an area of 3,468.4 sq mi (8,983 km2), with a large variety of lakes and ponds, canyons, rivers, and mountain ranges. Yellowstone Lake is one of the largest high-elevation lakes in North America and covers part of the Yellowstone Caldera, the largest super volcano on the continent. The caldera is considered a dormant volcano. It has erupted with tremendous force twice in the last two million years. Well over half of the world's geysers and hydrothermal features are in Yellowstone, fueled by this ongoing volcanism. Lava flows and rocks from volcanic eruptions cover most of the land area of Yellowstone. The park is the centerpiece of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the largest remaining nearly intact ecosystem in the Earth's northern temperate zone. In 1978, Yellowstone was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Hundreds of species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, and amphibians have been documented, including several that are either endangered or threatened. The vast forests and grasslands also include unique species of plants. Yellowstone Park is the largest and most famous megafauna location in the contiguous United States. The park is inhabited by grizzly bears, cougars, wolves, and free-ranging herds of bison and elk. The Yellowstone Park bison herd is the oldest and largest public bison herd in the United States. Forest fires occur in the park each year; in the large forest fires of 1988, over one-third of the park was burnt. Yellowstone has numerous recreational opportunities, including hiking, camping, boating, fishing, and sightseeing. Paved roads provide close access to the major geothermal areas as well as some of the lakes and waterfalls. During the winter, visitors often access the park by way of guided tours that use either snow coaches or snowmobiles in the snowy weather.

entries.title: Impressionism
entries.summary: Impressionism brought changing light, everyday subjects and visible brushwork into nineteenth-century painting. The independent exhibition of 1874 made these choices a public controversy and supplied the movement’s name through a satirical response to Claude Monet’s work.
body:
Impressionism was a nineteenth-century art movement that used visible brushstrokes, open compositions and unusual viewpoints to depict ordinary subjects. Painters paid close attention to changing light and the passage of time, treating movement as an essential part of how people perceive and experience the world. A group of Paris-based artists gained prominence through independent exhibitions in the 1870s and 1880s.

Their work met fierce opposition from France’s conventional art establishment. In a satirical review of the First Impressionist Exhibition in 1874, Louis Leroy coined the name from Claude Monet’s painting Impression, Sunrise. His review appeared in the Paris newspaper Le Charivari. Related approaches subsequently emerged in other media, becoming known as Impressionist music and literature.
story_headings: Light, movement and the name coined by a critic

provenance.date_note: First Impressionist Exhibition and naming of movement1874; not invention of the painting style in one day.
provenance.full_source_extract:
Impressionism was a 19th-century art movement characterised by visible brush strokes, open composition, emphasis on accurate depiction of light in its changing qualities (often accentuating the effects of the passage of time), ordinary subject matter, unusual visual angles, and inclusion of movement as a crucial element of human perception and experience. Impressionism originated with a group of Paris-based artists whose independent exhibitions brought them to prominence during the 1870s and 1880s.
The Impressionists faced harsh opposition from the conventional art community in France. The name of the style derives from the title of a Claude Monet work, Impression, Sunrise, which provoked the critic Louis Leroy to coin the term in a satirical 1874 review of the First Impressionist Exhibition published in the Parisian newspaper Le Charivari. The development of Impressionism in the visual arts was soon followed by analogous styles in other media that became known as Impressionist music and Impressionist literature.

entries.title: Organised ice hockey moves indoors
entries.subtitle: A scheduled match at Montreal’s Victoria Rink
entries.summary: James George Aylwin Creighton organised a public indoor ice-hockey match in Montreal on 3 March 1875. Named teams, a scheduled contest and newspaper coverage helped give the developing sport a more formal place before spectators.
body:
James George Aylwin Creighton organised an indoor ice-hockey match at Montreal’s Victoria Skating Rink on 3 March 1875. Two teams of nine players competed before spectators, using a flattened wooden disc. Creighton’s side beat Charles Torrance’s team two goals to one.

A newspaper announcement and a report after the match documented the occasion. Bringing named teams, a scheduled contest and an audience together at the rink helped establish organised ice hockey as the sport continued to develop in Montreal.
story_headings: Nine players a side at the Victoria Skating Rink

entries.title: Telephone
entries.summary: The telephone carries speech between people too far apart to hear one another directly. Alexander Graham Bell received its first US patent in 1876, and continued development brought the device into businesses, government offices and homes.
body:
A telephone allows two or more people to converse across a distance. It converts sound, especially the human voice, into electrical signals that travel through cables or other communication channels. A receiving telephone turns those signals back into sound for the listener. Its name combines the Ancient Greek τῆλε, tēle, meaning “far”, and φωνή, phōnē, meaning “voice”: a distant voice.

In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell received the first US telephone patent. His work demonstrated intelligible speech reproduced at a second instrument. Many others developed the device further, and it quickly became an essential means of communication in businesses, government and homes.
story_headings: Turning a voice into signals and back into sound

provenance.date_note: Bell granted United States telephone patent1876; do not call him sole inventor of all telephone technology.
provenance.full_source_extract:
A telephone, commonly shortened to phone, is a telecommunications device that enables two or more users to conduct a conversation when they are too far apart to be easily heard directly. A telephone converts sound, typically and most efficiently the human voice, into electronic signals that are transmitted via cables and other communication channels to another telephone which reproduces the sound to the receiving user. The term is derived from Ancient Greek: τῆλε, romanized: tēle, lit. 'far' and φωνή (phōnē, voice), together meaning distant voice.
In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell was the first to be granted a United States patent for a device that produced clearly intelligible replication of the human voice at a second device. This instrument was further developed by many others, and became rapidly indispensable in business, government, and in households.
The essential elements of a telephone are a microphone (transmitter) to speak into and an earphone (receiver) which reproduces the voice at a distant location. The receiver and transmitter are usually built into a handset which is held up to the ear and mouth during conversation. The transmitter converts the sound waves to electrical signals which are sent through the telecommunications system to the receiving telephone, which converts the signals into audible sound in the receiver or sometimes a loudspeaker. Telephones permit transmission in both directions simultaneously.
Most telephones also contain an alerting feature, such as a ringer or a visual indicator, to announce an incoming telephone call. Telephone calls are initiated most commonly with a keypad or dial, affixed to the telephone, to enter a telephone number, which is the address of the call recipient's telephone in the telecommunications system, but other methods existed in the early history of the telephone.
The first telephones were directly connected to each other from one customer's office or residence to another customer's location. Being impractical beyond just a few customers, these systems were quickly replaced by manually operated centrally located switchboards. These exchanges were soon connected together, eventually forming an automated, worldwide public switched telephone network. For greater mobility, various radio systems were developed in the mid-20th century for transmission between mobile stations on ships and in automobiles.
Handheld mobile phones were introduced for personal service starting in 1973. In later decades, the analog cellular system evolved into digital networks with greater capability and lower cost. Convergence in communication services has provided a broad spectrum of capabilities in cell phones, including mobile computing, giving rise to the smartphone, the dominant type of telephone in the world today.
Modern telephones exist in various forms and are implemented through different systems, including fixed-line, cellular, satellite, and Internet-based devices, all of which are integrated into the public switched telephone network (PSTN). This interconnected system allows any telephone, regardless of its underlying technology or geographic location, to reach another through a unique telephone number. While mobile and landline services are fully integrated into the global telecommunication network, some Internet-based services, such as VoIP, may not always be directly connected to the PSTN, though they still allow communication across different systems when a connection is made.

entries.title: Phonograph
entries.summary: Thomas Edison’s phonograph of 1877 recorded sound as physical variations in a groove and reproduced it with a stylus. Later improvements to recording surfaces and mechanisms helped establish the family of devices that includes gramophones and record players.
body:
Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877, creating a device for mechanically recording and reproducing sound in analogue form. The wider family of sound-reproduction machines came to include gramophones; from the 1940s, record player became a familiar term, alongside the later use of turntable.

Sound vibrations are represented by physical variations in a helical groove around a rotating cylinder or a spiral groove on a disc. The groove can be engraved, etched, cut or impressed into the surface. During playback, the record rotates and a stylus follows the groove, vibrating in response to its shape. Early acoustic machines used these vibrations to move a diaphragm, which produced sound carried into the air by a flaring horn or directly to the ears through stethoscope-like earphones.

In the 1880s, Alexander Graham Bell’s Volta Laboratory introduced improvements through the graphophone, including wax-coated cardboard cylinders. A cutting stylus recorded the sound as changes in the depth of the cylinder’s helical groove.
story_headings: A stylus turns the shape of a groove into sound

provenance.full_source_extract:
A phonograph, later called a gramophone, and since the 1940s a record player, or more recently a turntable, is a device for the mechanical and analogue reproduction of sound.
The sound vibration waveforms are recorded as corresponding physical deviations of a helical or spiral groove engraved, etched, incised, or impressed into the surface of a rotating cylinder or disc, called a record. To recreate the sound, the surface is similarly rotated while a playback stylus traces the groove and is therefore vibrated by it, faintly reproducing the recorded sound. In early acoustic phonographs, the stylus vibrated a diaphragm that produced sound waves coupled to the open air through a flaring horn, or directly to the listener's ears through stethoscope-type earphones.
The phonograph was invented in 1877 by Thomas Edison; Alexander Graham Bell's Volta Laboratory made several improvements in the 1880s and introduced the graphophone, including the use of wax-coated cardboard cylinders and a cutting stylus that moved from side to side in a helical groove around the record. In the 1890s, Emile Berliner initiated the transition from phonograph cylinders to flat discs with a spiral groove running from the periphery to near the centre, coining the term gramophone for disc record players, which is predominantly used in many languages. Later improvements through the years included modifications to the turntable and its drive system, stylus, pickup system, and the sound and equalization systems.
The disk phonograph record was the dominant commercial audio distribution format throughout most of the 20th century, and phonographs became the first example of home audio that people owned and used at their residences. In the 1960s, the use of 8-track cartridges and cassette tapes were introduced as alternatives. In the 1980s, phonograph use declined sharply due to the popularity of cassettes and the rise of the compact disc. However, records have undergone a revival since the late 2000s.

entries.title: Praxinoscope
entries.summary: Charles-Émile Reynaud’s praxinoscope, invented in France in 1877, used mirrors to animate a strip of pictures inside a rotating cylinder. It developed the zoetrope’s principle while giving viewers a brighter image with less distortion.
body:
The praxinoscope is an animation device invented in France by Charles-Émile Reynaud in 1877 as a successor to the zoetrope. Both place a strip of pictures around the inside of a spinning cylinder. Reynaud replaced the zoetrope’s narrow viewing slits with an inner ring of mirrors.

The mirrors are positioned so that each picture’s reflection appears in roughly the same place as the cylinder turns. Looking into them, the viewer sees images follow one another rapidly and merge into an illusion of movement. The picture is brighter and less distorted than the view through a zoetrope’s slits.
story_headings: Mirrors hold a moving sequence in view

Like the zoetrope, it uses a strip of pictures placed around the inner surface of a spinning cylinder. The praxinoscope improved on the zoetrope by replacing its narrow viewing slits with an inner circle of mirrors, placed so that the reflections of the pictures appeared more or less stationary in position as the wheel turned. Someone looking in the mirrors can, therefore, see a rapid succession of images producing the illusion of motion, with a brighter and less distorted picture than the zoetrope offered.

entries.title: The Horse in Motion
entries.summary: Eadweard Muybridge’s The Horse in Motion recorded successive phases of a horse’s movement in June 1878. Published as photographic cards, the sequences helped make motion available for scientific study and became an important precursor of moving pictures.
body:
The Horse in Motion is a series of cabinet cards by Eadweard Muybridge, including six cards with sequences of six to twelve “automatic electro-photographs” taken in June 1878. An additional card reproduced the single photograph of Occident trotting at speed that had already appeared in 1877.

The series was an early example of chronophotography: recording successive moments photographically to study the phases of movement. It became an influential step towards motion pictures, and one card, often titled Sallie Gardner at a Gallop, is especially associated with cinema’s beginnings.

From 1880 to 1895, Muybridge projected moving images with his zoopraxiscope, using pictures painted on discs from his photographs. This was distinct from projecting a photographic film. Projection of animated pictures already had precedents, including Franz von Uchatius’s work in 1853.
story_headings: Successive photographs reveal the phases of a horse’s movement

provenance.date_note: Muybridge horse photographic series shotJune1878.
provenance.full_source_extract:
The Horse in Motion is a series of cabinet cards by Eadweard Muybridge, including six cards that each show a series of six to twelve "automatic electro-photographs" depicting successive phases in the movement of a horse, shot in June 1878. An additional card reprinted the single image of the horse "Occident" trotting at high speed, which had already been published in 1877.
The series became the first example of chronophotography, an early method to photographically record the passing of time, mainly used to document the different phases of locomotion for scientific study. It formed a very influential step in the development of motion pictures. One of the cards (often retitled Sallie Gardner at a Gallop) has even been hailed as "the world's first bit of cinema". Muybridge did project moving images from his photographs with his zoopraxiscope, from 1880 to 1895, but these were painted on discs and his technology was no more advanced than earlier efforts by others (for instance those by Franz von Uchatius in 1853).
Muybridge's work was commissioned by Leland Stanford, the industrialist, former Governor of California, and horseman, who was interested in horse gait analysis. Stanford was personally convinced that contemporary depictions of running horses portrayed the animal incorrectly, and he wished to prove the issue scientifically. 
In 1882, Stanford had a book published about the project, also titled The Horse in Motion, with circa 100 plates of silhouettes based on the photographs, and analytical text by his physician and personal friend J.D.B. Stillman.
Muybridge continued his chronophotographic studies at the University of Pennsylvania, published the results as Animal Locomotion in 1887, and kept on lecturing about his work across the United States and Europe until his retirement around 1896.

entries.title: Edison’s carbon-filament lamp
entries.summary: Thomas Edison successfully tested a carbon-filament incandescent lamp in October 1879. Part of a longer development involving Joseph Swan and others, it made electric lighting depend on a practical lamp as well as the connections and supply that powered it.
body:
Thomas Edison successfully tested his carbon-filament incandescent lamp in October 1879. An electric current heated the filament until it glowed, while the glass bulb protected the material from oxidation. The work belonged to a longer development involving Joseph Swan and other inventors.

A practical, inexpensive lamp could bring electric lighting into homes and businesses, and later into portable lamps, vehicles and illuminated signs. Keeping the filament glowing required electrical connections and a sustained supply, linking the bulb to the system that powered it.
story_headings: A glowing filament needs a sustained electrical supply

provenance.date_note: Commercialization section identifies successful Edison carbon-filament test22October1879; earlier Swan and other lamp development is explicitly retained. This is not sole-inventor or first-electric-light claim.
provenance.full_source_extract:
An incandescent light bulb, also known as an incandescent lamp or incandescent light globe, is an electric light that produces illumination by Joule heating a filament until it glows. The filament is enclosed in a glass bulb that is either evacuated or filled with inert gas to protect the filament from oxidation. Electric current is supplied to the filament by terminals or wires embedded in the glass. A bulb socket provides mechanical support and electrical connections.
Incandescent bulbs are manufactured in a wide range of sizes, light output, and voltage ratings, from 1.5 volts to about 300 volts. They require no external regulating equipment, have low manufacturing costs, and work equally well on either alternating current or direct current. As a result, the incandescent bulb became widely used in household and commercial lighting, for portable lighting such as table lamps, car headlamps, and flashlights, and for decorative and advertising lighting.
Incandescent bulbs are much less efficient than other types of electric lighting. Less than 5% of the energy they consume is converted into visible light; the rest is released as heat. The luminous efficacy of a typical incandescent bulb is 16 lumens per watt (lm/W) for a 120 V bulb or 13 lm/W for a 230 V bulb, compared with 60 lm/W for a compact fluorescent bulb or 100 lm/W for typical white LED lamps. As a result, incandescent bulbs have declined in market share compared to LED bulbs. This has been accelerated by government bans aimed at reducing energy consumption. These bans have been controversial in some cases.

entries.title: Pablo Picasso
entries.summary: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist born in Málaga on 25 October 1881.
body: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist born in Málaga on 25 October 1881. Working mainly in France, he moved between painting, sculpture, printmaking and ceramics throughout a long career. His early Blue and Rose periods gave way to experiments in which bodies and objects were broken into angular forms. With Georges Braque, he developed Cubism, using overlapping planes and, later, collage to reconsider how a picture could organise things seen and understood from different positions.

Guernica, painted in 1937 for the Spanish Republic’s pavilion in Paris, responds to the bombing of the Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. Picasso builds the large scene with a restricted black, white and grey palette. A fallen figure, a wounded horse and people crying out fill a compressed interior, without becoming a straightforward illustration of the attack. The painting brings his earlier experiments with fractured bodies into a public work about violence and civilian suffering.

entries.title: Pearl Street Station begins supplying electricity
entries.summary: Pearl Street Station brought commercial electricity supply to its first Manhattan customers on 4 September 1882. Built by the Edison Illuminating Company, the plant connected electrical generation to the everyday use of lamps in a city district.
body:
Pearl Street Station began supplying electricity in Manhattan on 4 September 1882, initially serving 82 customers and around 400 lamps. It was Thomas Edison’s first commercial power station in the United States.

The Edison Illuminating Company built it under the direction of Francis Upton, whom Edison had hired. With a direct-current generating capacity of 600 kW, the plant occupied a site measuring 50 by 100 feet, or about 15 by 30 metres. It stood at 255–257 Pearl Street, just south of Fulton Street in New York City’s Financial District.
story_headings: Eighty-two customers supplied from a Manhattan power station

entries.title: Umberto Boccioni
entries.summary: Umberto Boccioni was an Italian painter and sculptor born in Reggio Calabria on 19 October 1882.
body: Umberto Boccioni was an Italian painter and sculptor born in Reggio Calabria on 19 October 1882. He became a central participant in Futurism, the movement that sought artistic forms for the speed and industrial transformation of modern life. His paintings of streets, stations and building sites organise figures and surroundings through intersecting directions. In The City Rises, workers and horses fill a construction scene whose dense movement makes the changing city part of the subject rather than a neutral background.

Unique Forms of Continuity in Space, modelled in plaster in 1913, extends that inquiry into sculpture. A striding figure expands into curved surfaces that suggest movement through the surrounding air. The form does not simply describe a body caught at a single instant; it connects the figure to the space through which it moves. Familiar bronze versions were cast after Boccioni’s death, so the material and casting date distinguish those objects from the original plaster model.

entries.title: Nipkow disk
entries.summary: The Nipkow disk made mechanical image scanning central to early television. Paul Gottlieb Nipkow's patent took effect in 1884, decades before versions of his rotating device appeared in television systems of the 1920s and 1930s.
body: The Nipkow disk is a rotating mechanical device that scans an image through the geometry of its movement. Also called a scanning disk, and sometimes spelled Nipkov in English, it was patented by Paul Gottlieb Nipkow in Berlin. The patent was granted on 15 January 1885 with effect from 6 January 1884. The design later became a fundamental component of mechanical television, used in early television systems during the 1920s and 1930s.
story_headings: A patent ahead of television

entries.title: Statue of Liberty
entries.summary: The Statue of Liberty was dedicated in New York Harbor on 28 October 1886. Its torch, inscribed tablet and broken chain brought independence and the abolition of slavery into the imagery of a gift from France.
body:
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical sculpture on Liberty Island in New York City, overlooking New York Harbor. Its full name is Liberty Enlightening the World, or La Liberté éclairant le monde in French; Lady Liberty is its familiar nickname. The people of France gave the copper-clad statue to the United States. French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi designed it, Gustave Eiffel built its metal framework, and it was dedicated on 28 October 1886.

The crowned woman in classical robes draws on Libertas, the Roman goddess of liberty. She raises a torch in her right hand and holds a tabula ansata, a tablet with projecting handles, in her left. Its inscription, JULY IV MDCCLXXVI, gives 4 July 1776, the date of the United States Declaration of Independence, in Roman numerals. At her left foot, a broken chain and shackle commemorate the nationwide abolition of slavery following the American Civil War.
story_headings: Liberty, independence and a broken chain

The Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World, French: La Liberté éclairant le monde; colloquially known as Lady Liberty) is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed and crowned woman on Liberty Island, part of New York City, in New York Harbor. The copper-clad statue, a gift to the United States from the people of France, was designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, and its metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel. The statue was dedicated on October 28, 1886.
The statue is a figure of a classically draped woman, inspired by the Roman goddess of liberty, Libertas. She holds a torch above her head with her right hand, and in her left hand carries a tabula ansata inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI (July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals), the date of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. With her left foot she steps on a broken chain and shackle, commemorating the national abolition of slavery following the American Civil War.
In 1865, the French historian and abolitionist Édouard de Laboulaye proposed a monument to commemorate the upcoming centennial of U.S. independence (1876), the perseverance of American democracy and the liberation of the nation's slaves. The Franco-Prussian War delayed progress until 1875, when Laboulaye proposed that the people of France finance the statue and the United States provide the site and build the pedestal. Bartholdi completed the head and the torch-bearing arm before the statue was fully designed, and these pieces were exhibited for publicity at international expositions. The torch-bearing arm was displayed at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia in 1876, and in Madison Square Park in Manhattan from 1876 to 1882. Fundraising proved difficult, especially for the Americans; publisher Joseph Pulitzer of the New York World started a drive for donations to finish the project. The statue was built in France, shipped overseas in crates, and assembled on the completed pedestal on what was then called Bedloe's Island. The statue's completion was marked by New York's first ticker-tape parade and a dedication ceremony presided over by President Grover Cleveland.
The statue became an icon of freedom and of the United States, seen as a symbol of welcome to immigrants arriving by sea. The statue was administered by the United States Lighthouse Board until 1901 and then by the Department of War; since 1933, it has been maintained by the National Park Service as part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument, and is a major tourist attraction. Limited numbers of visitors can access the rim of the pedestal and the interior of the statue's crown from within; public access to the torch has been barred since 1916.

entries.title: Michelson–Morley experiment
entries.summary: The Michelson–Morley experiment compared light travelling in perpendicular directions to test Earth's motion through the proposed luminiferous aether. Its 1887 result challenged that explanation of light and contributed to the research that led towards special relativity.
body:
Albert Michelson and Edward Morley carried out their light experiment in Cleveland between April and July 1887 and published the results that November. They compared light travelling in perpendicular directions, looking for a difference caused by Earth's movement through the supposed luminiferous aether, the medium thought to carry light waves. No significant difference appeared.

The result challenged aether theories and encouraged further investigation into light and motion. This work formed part of the scientific path towards special relativity, which would describe their relationship without requiring motion relative to an aether.
story_headings: An expected difference that did not appear

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Michelson–Morley experiment was an attempt to measure the motion of the Earth relative to the luminiferous aether, a supposed medium permeating space that was thought to be the carrier of light waves.  The experiment was performed between April and July 1887 by American physicists Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley at what is now Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, and published in November of the same year.
The experiment compared the speed of light in perpendicular directions in an attempt to detect the relative motion of matter, including their laboratory, through the luminiferous aether, or "aether wind" as it was sometimes called. The result was negative, in that Michelson and Morley found no significant difference between the speed of light in the direction of movement through the presumed aether, and the speed at right angles. This result is generally considered to be the first strong evidence against some aether theories, as well as initiating a line of research that eventually led to special relativity, which rules out motion against an aether. Of this experiment, Albert Einstein wrote, "If the Michelson–Morley experiment had not brought us into serious embarrassment, no one would have regarded the relativity theory as a (halfway) redemption."
Michelson–Morley type experiments have been repeated many times with steadily increasing sensitivity. These include experiments from 1902 to 1905, and a series of experiments in the 1920s. More recently, in 2009, optical resonator experiments confirmed the absence of any aether wind at the 10−17 level. Together with the Ives–Stilwell and Kennedy–Thorndike experiments, Michelson–Morley type experiments form one of the fundamental tests of special relativity.

entries.title: Marcel Duchamp
entries.summary: Marcel Duchamp was a French-born artist born near Blainville on 28 July 1887.
body: Marcel Duchamp was a French-born artist born near Blainville on 28 July 1887. He began as a painter, examining movement in works such as Nude Descending a Staircase, before making selection and presentation central to his practice. His readymades were manufactured objects placed in an artistic context rather than modelled or painted by hand. Their titles and altered settings asked viewers to consider how an ordinary thing became an artwork, and who had the authority to make that decision.

In 1917 a urinal signed R. Mutt was submitted as Fountain to an exhibition in New York and was not displayed. The original object disappeared, but Alfred Stieglitz’s photograph and later authorised replicas preserved its appearance. This distinction matters when viewing the work in a museum: the displayed version may be a later reconstruction rather than the 1917 object. Duchamp’s challenge concerned the choice and context of the object, not simply the shock of its unusual subject.

entries.title: Benz Patent-Motorwagen

date.region: Europe; commercial sales documented in Germany/France

entries.summary: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen brought a practical petrol engine and transmission together in a three-wheeled car. Completed in 1885 and subsequently developed for sale, it established a mechanical layout that Benz continued to refine in later vehicles.
body:
The Benz Patent-Motorwagen, whose name means patent motorcar, is widely regarded as the first practical automobile. German engineer Carl Benz developed the original design between 1884 and 1887, completing a vehicle in 1885. Commercial sales followed by 1888; the three-wheeled models built by Benz & Cie through 1893 combined a single-cylinder, four-stroke engine with belt transmission.

Benz also used the Patent-Motorwagen name for four-wheeled cars until around 1900, including vehicles now better known as the Viktoria and Velo. They retained the basic layout and belt-drive technology covered by patent DRP37435, granted in 1886.

A flywheel evened out the engine's output. Early vehicles had a horizontal flywheel and a single drive belt; later versions used a vertical flywheel and two belts. Each belt provided one transmission ratio. From 1886, the single-belt vehicles also had reduction gearing that supplied a second ratio.
story_headings: From the 1885 vehicle to commercial production

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Benz Patent-Motorwagen ("patent motorcar") was the world's first practical production automobile, built by Benz & Cie between 1885 and 1893. Featuring three wheels, a single-cylinder four-stroke engine and belt-drive, Benz & Cie used the designation "Patent-Motorwagen" for their four-wheel cars until c.1900, but these are known today by their other names, such as Viktoria and Velo. All these cars used the same layout and belt-drive technology for which Benz received patent number DRP37435 in 1886, hence the designation.
The original Patent-Motorwagen was developed over the period 1884 – 1887 by the German engineer Carl Benz and is widely regarded as the first practical automobile.
The engine's output was stabilised by a flywheel. In the first vehicles this was horizontal and the vehicles had a single belt-drive. Later vehicles had a vertical flywheel and two belt-drives. Each belt-drive gave a single transmission ratio; from 1886 the single-belt-drive vehicles also had a reduction gearbox which provided a second transmission ratio.
Production ceased after Benz had perfected two-wheel steering and began manufacturing four-wheel models from late 1892. Around 1895 the Sales Manager at Benz & Cie sought to recreate the form which the original vehicle took in early 1886 before it was given a new body. The rebuilt vehicle was given to the Deutsches Museum in 1906; replicas of it have been produced from the mid-twentieth century.

entries.title: Tesla's alternating-current motor patents
entries.summary: Tesla's motor patents of May 1888 belong to the development of alternating-current power, alongside Galileo Ferraris's independent work. Rotating magnetic fields offered a way to turn electrical energy into the motion of a motor shaft.
body:
Nikola Tesla received patents for his alternating-current motor system in May 1888 and presented the work that month. Galileo Ferraris independently worked on motors based on a rotating magnetic field.

An alternating-current, or AC, motor generally has two main parts: an outer, stationary stator and an inner rotor attached to the output shaft. Alternating current in the stator's coils produces a rotating magnetic field. Depending on the design, the rotor interacts with this field through permanent magnets, electrical windings carrying direct or alternating current, or a shape that gives magnetic flux an easier path in some directions than others. This last arrangement produces reluctance torque.

Less common linear AC motors use similar principles, but arrange their stationary and moving parts along a straight line. Their output is linear movement rather than rotation.
story_headings: How alternating current turns a shaft

provenance.full_source_extract:
An AC motor is an electric motor driven by an alternating current (AC). The AC motor commonly consists of two basic parts, an outside stator having coils supplied with alternating current to produce a rotating magnetic field, and an inside rotor attached to the output shaft producing a second rotating magnetic field. The rotor magnetic field may be produced by permanent magnets, reluctance saliency, or DC or AC electrical windings.
Less common, AC linear motors operate on similar principles as rotating motors but have their stationary and moving parts arranged in a straight line configuration, producing linear motion instead of rotation.

entries.title: The Kodak camera arrives
entries.summary: The Kodak camera of 1888 linked an accessible consumer camera to a growing business in photographic film. Later Brownie and Instamatic models continued an approach that made photography available to a much wider public.
body:
The Kodak camera appeared in 1888, bringing roll-film photography to a wider public. George Eastman and Henry A. Strong had formed the partnership behind its development; Eastman Kodak was incorporated in 1892. Film became the centre of a business that grew into one of the world's largest photographic manufacturers.

The later Brownie and Instamatic cameras continued this emphasis on a broad consumer market. The 1888 model established the relationship between a simple camera and the photographic-film industry that supplied it.

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Eastman Kodak Company, referred to simply as Kodak ( ), is an American public company that produces various products related to its historic roots in film photography. The company is headquartered in Rochester, New York, and is incorporated in New Jersey. It is best known for photographic film products, which it brought to a mass market for the first time.
Kodak began as a partnership between George Eastman and Henry A. Strong to develop a film roll camera. After the release of the Kodak camera, Eastman Kodak was incorporated on May 23, 1892. Under Eastman's direction, the company became one of the world's largest film and camera manufacturers, and also developed a model of welfare capitalism and a close relationship with the city of Rochester. During most of the 20th century, Kodak held a dominant position in photographic film, and produced several technological innovations through heavy investment in research and development at Kodak Research Laboratories. Kodak produced some of the most popular camera models of the 20th century, including the Brownie and Instamatic. The company's ubiquity was such that its "Kodak moment" tagline entered the common lexicon to describe a personal event that deserved to be recorded for posterity.
Kodak began to struggle financially in the late 1990s as a result of increasing competition from Fujifilm. The company also struggled with the transition from film to digital photography, even though Kodak had invented integral color image sensors and had developed the first self-contained digital camera prototype in the mid-1970s. Attempts to diversify its chemical operations failed, and as a turnaround strategy in the 2000s, Kodak instead made an aggressive turn to digital photography and digital printing. These strategies failed to improve the company's finances, and in January 2012, Kodak filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York.
In September 2013, the company emerged from bankruptcy, having shed its large legacy liabilities, restructured, and exited several businesses. Since emerging from bankruptcy, Kodak has continued to provide commercial digital printing products and services, motion picture film, and still film, the last of which was distributed through the spinoff company Kodak Alaris until 2026. The company has licensed the Kodak brand to several products produced by other companies, such as the PIXPRO line of digital cameras manufactured by JK Imaging, and in the 2020s has expanded into the health sector with the opening of a pharmaceuticals production facility.

entries.title: Giorgio de Chirico
entries.summary: Giorgio de Chirico was an Italian artist born in Volos, Greece, on 10 July 1888.
body: Giorgio de Chirico was an Italian artist born in Volos, Greece, on 10 July 1888. His early training in Greece and Munich preceded the paintings he developed in Italy and Paris. Empty squares, arcades, statues and long shadows became features of his Metaphysical painting. These are recognisable things, but their proportions, perspectives and combinations can make a scene difficult to place. The work offered an important example to later Surrealist artists without depending on the depiction of an actual dream.

The Song of Love, painted in 1914, brings together a classical sculpted head, a large rubber glove and a green ball, with a train visible beyond a wall. Each object is clearly drawn, yet the arrangement gives no ordinary reason for their presence together. The painting connects ancient sculpture, modern manufactured objects and railway imagery within one constructed space. De Chirico later pursued different approaches to painting and revisited earlier subjects, so his long career extends beyond the celebrated early squares.

entries.title: Eiffel Tower
entries.summary: The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair and the centenary of the French Revolution. A disputed addition to Paris at first, its exposed iron structure became a widely recognised image of France.
body:
The Eiffel Tower, or Tour Eiffel, is an iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It takes its name from engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built it between 1887 and 1889. Its puddled-iron structure earned it the local nickname La dame de fer, the Iron Lady.

The tower formed the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair, marking a hundred years since the French Revolution. Some leading French artists and intellectuals initially criticised its design. It subsequently became a cultural symbol of France and one of the world's most recognisable buildings.

Operator SETE's financial figures record 6.192 million visitors in 2022; its report for 2015 recorded 6.917 million. Guinness World Records identifies it as the world's most visited monument charging admission, citing its 2014 attendance. The tower became a monument historique in 1964 and, in 1991, part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Paris, Banks of the Seine.

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Eiffel Tower (  EYE-fəl; French: Tour Eiffel [tuʁ ɛfɛl] ) is a lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower from 1887 to 1889.
Locally nicknamed "La dame de fer" (French for "Iron Lady") for its use of wrought iron, it was constructed as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair, and to crown the centennial anniversary of the French Revolution. Although initially criticised by some of France's leading artists and intellectuals for its design, it has since become a global cultural icon of France and one of the most recognisable structures in the world. The tower received 5,889,000 visitors in 2022. The Eiffel Tower is the most visited monument with an entrance fee in the world: 6.91 million people ascended it in 2015. It was designated a monument historique in 1964, and was named part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site ("Paris, Banks of the Seine") in 1991.
The tower is 330 metres (1,083 ft) tall, about the same height as an 81-storey building, and the tallest structure in Paris. Its base is square, measuring 125 metres (410 ft) on each side. During its construction, the Eiffel Tower surpassed the Washington Monument to become by far the tallest human-made structure in the world, a title it held for 41 years until the Chrysler Building in New York City was finished in 1930. It was the first structure in the world to surpass both the 200-metre and 300-metre mark in height. Due to the addition of a broadcasting aerial at the top of the tower in 1957, it is now taller than the Chrysler Building by 11 metres (36 ft). Excluding transmitters, the Eiffel Tower is the second tallest free-standing structure in France after the Millau Viaduct.
The tower has three levels for visitors, with restaurants on the first and second levels. The top level's upper platform is 276 m (906 ft) above the ground—the highest public observation deck in the European Union. Tickets can be purchased to ascend by stairs or lift to the first and second levels. The climb from ground level to the first level is over 300 steps, as is the climb from the first level to the second, making the entire ascent a 600-step climb. Although there is a staircase to the top level, it is usually accessible only by lift. On this top, third level, is a private apartment built for Gustave Eiffel, who decorated it with furniture made by Jean Lachaise and invited friends such as Thomas Edison.

entries.title: Charlie Chaplin
entries.subtitle: Born in London, trained on the stage
entries.summary: Charlie Chaplin brought the timing of stage comedy to cinema and shaped his films as actor, director, writer and composer. The Tramp's instantly recognisable appearance made physical movement a way to convey dignity, embarrassment and affection.
body: Charles Spencer Chaplin was born in London on 16 April 1889. His childhood combined hardship with early experience of performing, and stage work eventually took him into cinema. As an actor, director, writer and composer, he came to exercise unusually close control over his films. Audiences could recognise the Tramp from his clothes and movements before learning anything about the character.

Chaplin trained in dance and comedy, and American tours with Fred Karno led him into motion pictures. The Tramp took shape in 1914. A small hat, cane, tight coat and oversized shoes gave him deliberately mismatched proportions, while his behaviour combined an effort to remain dignified with desperate improvisation. A meal, a doorway or a machine could set a scene in motion. Precisely timed physical actions then conveyed embarrassment, defiance or affection.

In The Kid, City Lights and Modern Times, sustained comic invention grew out of relationships marked by poverty, work and vulnerability. Chaplin continued to rely on gesture and music as sound cinema developed, then used speech for the final address in The Great Dictator.

He returned to the United States in 1972 to receive an honorary Academy Award. After an extended ovation, his brief, emotional response brought the performer face to face once more with audiences who had grown up with his films.

entries.title: Herman Hollerith: punched cards for the census
entries.summary: The 1890 United States census used Herman Hollerith's punched-card system to process its data. His tabulating machines helped establish mechanised data processing, while the company he founded became part of the business later named IBM.
body:
The 1890 United States census processed its data with Herman Hollerith's punched-card tabulating system. Hollerith, a German-American statistician, inventor and businessman, was born on 29 February 1860 and died on 17 November 1929. His electromechanical machine summarised information recorded on cards and later found a use in accounting.

Patent applications began in 1884; the key patents were granted on 8 January 1889. The system helped establish mechanised processing of information encoded by the presence or absence of holes, with some stages automated and others handled by operators. Punched-card methods continued to dominate this field for nearly a century, making Hollerith a central figure in the history of data processing.

His company joined several others in 1911 to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company. Renamed International Business Machines, or IBM, in 1924, it became one of the largest and most successful businesses of the twentieth century.

Herman Hollerith (February 29, 1860 – November 17, 1929) was a German-American statistician, inventor, and businessman who developed an electromechanical tabulating machine for punched cards to assist in summarizing information and, later, in accounting. His invention of the punched card tabulating machine, patented in 1884, marks the beginning of the era of mechanized binary code and semiautomatic data processing systems, and his concept dominated that landscape for nearly a century.
Hollerith founded a company that was amalgamated in 1911 with several other companies to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company. In 1924, the company was renamed "International Business Machines" (IBM) and became one of the largest and most successful companies of the 20th century. Hollerith is regarded as one of the seminal figures in the development of data processing.

entries.title: Naismith invents basketball
entries.subtitle: An indoor game for a New England winter
entries.summary: James Naismith devised basketball in Springfield in December 1891 to keep students active indoors during winter. Two peach baskets and thirteen rules established a game built around passing, with nine players on each of the first teams.
body:
James Naismith created basketball in December 1891 at the International YMCA Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts, now Springfield College. His supervisor, Luther Gulick, wanted an indoor activity that would hold students' interest through winter. Naismith provided a soccer ball, two peach baskets raised above the floor and thirteen rules.

The first game, dated 21 December by the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame, had nine players on each side. Passing was essential because players could not run with the ball. The rules appeared in the school magazine in January 1892, and students took the sport elsewhere. Later changes introduced dribbling and nets with open bottoms.
story_headings: Peach baskets and thirteen rules

entries.title: World's Columbian Exposition
entries.summary: The World's Columbian Exposition made Chicago a stage for architecture, industry and electric illumination in 1893. Its vast lighting installation gave alternating current a prominent public demonstration during the contest over how electricity should be distributed.
body:
The World's Columbian Exposition, also known as the Chicago World's Fair, ran from 1 May to 30 October 1893. It commemorated the four-hundredth anniversary of Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas in 1492. At the centre of the Jackson Park site, a large pool represented his Atlantic voyage. Chicago had won the hosting contest against cities including New York, Washington, D.C., and St. Louis. The fair influenced American architecture and the arts, encouraged confidence in industrial development and reshaped Chicago's public image.

Electric lighting was one of its major attractions. George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla's alternating-current system supplied a vast installation of more than 200,000 lamps. Winning the lighting contract was a major victory for AC in its rivalry with the direct-current technology associated with Thomas Edison. The fair demonstrated AC's potential for efficient power distribution and strengthened its position in the debate over long-distance transmission, while concerns about electrical safety continued.
story_headings: A world's fair illuminated by alternating current

provenance.date_note: Worlds Columbian Exposition opens1May1893; dedication ceremonies1892.
provenance.full_source_extract:
The World's Columbian Exposition, also known as the Chicago World's Fair, was a world's fair held in Chicago from May 1 to October 30, 1893, to celebrate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's arrival in the New World in 1492. The centerpiece of the fair, held in Jackson Park, was a large water pool representing the voyage that Columbus took to the New World. Chicago won the right to host the fair over several competing cities, including New York City, Washington, D.C., and St. Louis. The exposition was an influential social and cultural event and had a profound effect on American architecture, the arts, American industrial optimism, and Chicago's image.
A highlight was that Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse showcased their alternating current (AC) system, effectively winning the war of the currents against Thomas Edison's direct current (DC). The fair was the first all-electric, featuring over 200,000 lamps powered by Tesla's polyphase system, demonstrating its superior safety and efficiency for long-distance power distribution.
The layout of the Chicago Columbian Exposition was predominantly designed by John Wellborn Root, Daniel Burnham, Frederick Law Olmsted, and Charles B. Atwood. It was the prototype of what Burnham and his colleagues thought a city should be. It was designed to follow Beaux-Arts principles of design, namely neoclassical architecture principles based on symmetry, balance, and splendor. The color of the material generally used to cover the buildings' façades, white staff, gave the fairgrounds its nickname, the White City. Many prominent architects designed its 14 "great buildings". Artists and musicians were featured in exhibits and many also made depictions and works of art inspired by the exposition. One particularly notable attraction was the world's first Ferris wheel, standing at a height of 264 feet, which was designed to rival the Eiffel Tower built for the 1889 World's Fair four years earlier.
The exposition covered 690 acres (2.8 km2), featuring nearly 200 new but temporary buildings of predominantly neoclassical architecture, canals and lagoons, and people and cultures from 46 countries. More than 27 million people attended the exposition during its six-month run. Its scale and grandeur far exceeded the other world's fairs, and it became a symbol of supposed American exceptionalism, much in the same way that the Great Exhibition became a symbol of the Victorian era United Kingdom.
Dedication ceremonies for the fair were held on October 21, 1892, but the fairgrounds were not opened to the public until May 1, 1893. The fair continued until October 30, 1893. In addition to recognizing the 400th anniversary of the Europeans' discovery of the New World, the fair served to show the world that Chicago had risen from the ashes of the Great Chicago Fire, which had destroyed much of the city in 1871.
On October 9, 1893, the day designated as Chicago Day, the fair set a world record for outdoor event attendance, drawing 751,026 people. The debt for the fair was soon paid off with a check for $1.5 million (equivalent to $53.8 million in 2025). Chicago has commemorated the fair with one of the stars on its municipal flag.

entries.title: X-ray
entries.summary: X-rays, discovered by Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen in 1895, can pass through materials that stop visible light. This property made them useful for examining bodies and structures, while their ability to ionise matter required controls on exposure.
body:
X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation, discovered in 1895 by German scientist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen. He chose the letter X to indicate that the radiation's nature was unknown. Its wavelengths are shorter than ultraviolet wavelengths and generally longer than those in the gamma-ray band, although the boundaries between these bands are not sharp.

An approximate X-ray range runs from 10 nanometres to 10 picometres. This corresponds to frequencies of roughly 30 petahertz to 30 exahertz, or 3 × 10¹⁶ to 3 × 10¹⁹ hertz, and photon energies of about 100 electronvolts to 100 kiloelectronvolts.

X-rays penetrate many solid materials and living tissues. Radiography therefore became useful in medical diagnosis, including the examination of broken bones, and in materials science, where X-ray methods can identify elements and reveal weaknesses in structures. X-rays are also ionising radiation: exposure can damage DNA and increase cancer risk, while high doses can cause burns and radiation sickness. Health authorities regulate their production and use to control these risks.
story_headings: Penetrating matter with high-energy radiation

An X-ray is a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength shorter than those of ultraviolet rays and longer than those of gamma rays. Roughly, X-rays have a wavelength ranging from 10 nanometers to 10 picometers, corresponding to frequencies in the range of 30 petahertz to 30 exahertz (3×1016 Hz to 3×1019 Hz) and photon energies in the range of 100 eV to 100 keV, respectively.
X-rays were discovered in 1895 by the German scientist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who named it X-radiation to signify an unknown type of radiation.
X-rays can penetrate many solid substances such as construction materials and living tissue, so X-ray radiography is widely used in medical diagnostics  (e.g., checking for broken bones) and materials science (e.g., identification of some chemical elements and detecting weak points in construction materials).  However X-rays are ionizing radiation and exposure can be hazardous to health, causing DNA damage, cancer and, at higher intensities, burns and radiation sickness.  Their generation and use is strictly controlled by public health authorities.

entries.title: The Lumière brothers: the Cinématographe screenings
entries.summary: The Lumière brothers' Cinématographe brought moving pictures before shared audiences in 1895. Their Paris demonstrations culminated in a commercial public screening on 28 December, a date traditionally associated with the birth of cinema.
body:
Auguste and Louis Lumière were French manufacturers of photographic equipment whose Cinématographe system and short films placed them among cinema's earliest filmmakers. Auguste Marie Louis Nicolas Lumière lived from 19 October 1862 to 10 April 1954; Louis Jean Lumière from 5 October 1864 to 6 June 1948. Their film production spanned the years 1895 to 1905.

On 22 March 1895 they showed a single film to around 200 members of the Société d'encouragement pour l'industrie nationale, the Society for the Development of the National Industry, in Paris. It was an early demonstration of projected film to an assembled audience. Their first commercial public screening followed on 28 December. The Institut Lumière records thirty-three paying spectators, alongside invited guests and relations. That December screening has traditionally been treated as the birth of cinema.
story_headings: From an industrial society to a public screening

entries.title: Becquerel discovers radioactivity
entries.summary: Henri Becquerel's observation of radiation from uranium minerals in 1896 opened a new field of research. Radioactive decay revealed changes within atoms whose timing is unpredictable individually but measurable across large populations through their half-lives.
body:
Henri Becquerel observed uranium minerals spontaneously emitting radiation in 1896. The discovery opened an investigation into materials that release energy through changes inside their atoms. Radioactive decay occurs when an unstable nucleus loses energy, commonly through alpha, beta or gamma radiation.

The moment when an individual atom will decay cannot be predicted. Large groups, however, have measurable decay rates, expressed through a half-life: the time in which half of the unstable nuclei decay. These periods differ enormously between isotopes, from almost instantaneous changes to intervals longer than the age of the universe.
story_headings: An unpredictable atom, a measurable half-life

images.title: Photo of experimenters taking an X-ray with an early Crookes tube apparatus, from the late 1800s. The Crookes x-ray tube is visible suspended at center. The upper man is examining the bones of his hand with a fluoroscope screen. The lower man is taking a radiograph of his hand with a photographic plate . The power source is an induction coil , seen at left, and the mechanism immediately to its right against the wall is a motor-operated 'break wheel' interrupter in the coil's primary circuit. The large flat disk on the table is a rheostat (adjustable resistor) power control to adjust the primary current to the coil. Several spare Crookes X-ray tubes are seen in a rack on the wall. The apparatus is described and diagrammed on p.88 of the source. No precautions against radiation exposure are taken; its hazards were not known at the time. The original image was half-tone. Alterations: removed frame.

provenance.date_note: Atomic-theory history section explicitly places Becquerels observation of spontaneous mineral radiation in1896. This supports the proposed discovery milestone, not invention of radiation.
provenance.full_source_extract:
Radioactive decay (also known as nuclear decay, radioactivity, radioactive disintegration, or nuclear disintegration) is the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by radiation. A material containing unstable nuclei is considered radioactive. Three of the most common types of decay are alpha, beta, and gamma decay. The weak force is the mechanism that is responsible for beta decay, while the other two are governed by the electromagnetic and nuclear forces.
Radioactive decay is a random process at the level of single atoms. According to quantum theory, it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay, regardless of how long the atom has existed. However, for a significant number of identical atoms, the overall decay rate can be expressed as a decay constant or as a half-life. The half-lives of radioactive isotopes have a huge range: from nearly instantaneous to far longer than the age of the universe.
The decaying nucleus is called the parent radionuclide (or parent radioisotope), and the process produces at least one daughter nuclide. Except for gamma decay or internal conversion from a nuclear excited state, the decay is a nuclear transmutation resulting in a daughter containing a different number of protons or neutrons (or both). When the number of protons changes, an atom of a different chemical element is created.
There are 28 naturally occurring chemical elements on Earth that are radioactive, consisting of 35 radionuclides (seven elements have two different radionuclides each) that date before the time of formation of the Solar System. These 35 are known as primordial radionuclides. Well-known examples are uranium and thorium, but also included are naturally occurring long-lived radioisotopes, such as potassium-40. Each of the heavy primordial radionuclides participates in one of the four decay chains.

entries.title: Athens 1896 Olympics
entries.summary: The Athens Olympics of April 1896 revived the Games with an international field that was entirely male and mostly Greek. Their silver and copper prizes preceded the familiar medal rankings later applied retrospectively by the IOC.
body:
Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games from 6 to 15 April 1896. Organised by the International Olympic Committee established by Pierre de Coubertin, they drew competitors from fourteen countries according to the IOC's count. All the athletes were men, and most were Greek.

Winners received silver medals and runners-up copper. The IOC later assigned gold, silver and bronze rankings retrospectively. On the opening day, American triple jumper James Connolly became the first Olympic champion in more than fifteen centuries.
story_headings: Silver medals for the first modern champions
