provenance.full_source_extract:
Dragon Ball (Japanese: ドラゴンボール, Hepburn: Doragon Bōru) is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Akira Toriyama. Originally serialized in Shueisha's shōnen manga magazine Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1984 to 1995, the 519 individual chapters were collected in 42 tankōbon volumes. The story follows the adventures of Son Goku, from childhood to adulthood, as he trains in martial arts and explores the world in search of the Dragon Balls, seven magical orbs which summon a wish-granting dragon when gathered. Along his journey, Goku makes several friends and battles villains, many of whom also seek the Dragon Balls. Dragon Ball was inspired by the Chinese novel Journey to the West and Hong Kong martial arts films. It initially had a comedy focus but later became an action-packed fighting series. 
The original manga was adapted into three anime series produced by Toei Animation: Dragon Ball and Dragon Ball Z, which were broadcast in Japan from 1986 to 1996, and Dragon Ball Z Kai, a recut and remastered version of Z which was broadcast in Japan from 2009 to 2015. The series spawned a wider media franchise; among merchandise, there have been animated sequel and midquel series, both animated and live-action films, collectible trading card games, action figures, collections of soundtracks, and numerous video games. The series was licensed for an English-language release in North America and the United Kingdom by Viz Media, and in Australia and New Zealand by Madman Entertainment. The companies initially split the manga into two parts, Dragon Ball and Dragon Ball Z to match the anime series, but the most recent edition of the series was released in full under its original title.
Dragon Ball became one of the most successful manga series of all time. Its initial serialization in Weekly Shōnen Jump was partly responsible for the magazine reaching its highest circulation of 6.53 million weekly sales. Its collected tankōbon volumes have 160 million copies sold in Japan and 260 million sold worldwide, making it one of the best-selling manga series of all time. Reviewers have praised the manga for its comedy, fight scenes, and pacing, while recognizing a coming-of-age theme and its use of cultural references from Chinese mythology and Japanese folktales. Complaints from parents in the United States resulted in English-language releases being edited to remove nudity, racial stereotypes, and other content.
Also regarded as one of the most influential manga series, Dragon Ball has inspired numerous manga artists, including Eiichiro Oda (One Piece), Masashi Kishimoto (Naruto), and Tite Kubo (Bleach). A midquel series, titled Dragon Ball Super, has been published in V Jump since 2015. It was written by Toriyama and illustrated by Toyotarou.

entries.title: Atari ST
entries.summary: The Atari ST followed the company's 8-bit computers with a mouse-controlled graphical desktop and a Motorola 68000 processor. Developed by a small team after Jack Tramiel's takeover, the range combined a new computing environment with aggressive memory pricing.
body:
The Atari ST succeeded Atari's 8-bit computer family. Its first model, the 520ST, was already on shop shelves in Canada and parts of Western Europe by June 1985, with American specialist-store distribution following in July. Developer machines had circulated earlier that spring. The ST used a bitmapped colour graphical interface based on Digital Research's GEM, an environment available for other computers by February 1985. In 1986, the 1040ST supplied 1 MB of RAM at a price below one US dollar per kilobyte, a threshold contemporary coverage identified as a first for a personal computer.

Jack Tramiel acquired Atari, Inc.'s consumer-division assets in 1984 to form Atari Corporation. A small team led by Shiraz Shivji developed the 520ST in about five months. Alongside the Macintosh, Amiga, Apple IIGS and Archimedes, it belonged to a generation of machines with 16- or 32-bit processors, at least 256 KB of RAM and graphical interfaces controlled by a mouse. ST officially meant Sixteen/Thirty-two, referring to the Motorola 68000's 16-bit external bus and 32-bit internal architecture.
story_headings: A new computer after the takeover

provenance.full_source_extract:
Atari ST is a line of personal computers from Atari Corporation and the successor to the company's 8-bit computers. The initial model, the Atari 520ST, had limited release in April–June 1985, and was widely available in July. It was the first personal computer with a bitmapped color graphical user interface, using a version of Digital Research's GEM environment from February 1985. The Atari 1040ST, released in 1986 with 1 MB of memory, was the first home computer with a cost per kilobyte of RAM under US$1/KB.
After Jack Tramiel purchased the assets of the Atari, Inc. consumer division in 1984 to create Atari Corporation, the 520ST was designed in five months by a small team led by Shiraz Shivji. Alongside the Macintosh, Amiga, Apple IIGS, and Archimedes, the ST is part of a mid-1980s generation of computers with 16 or 32-bit processors, 256 KB or more of RAM, and mouse-controlled graphical user interfaces. "ST" officially stands for "Sixteen/Thirty-two", referring to the Motorola 68000's 16-bit external bus and 32-bit internals.
The ST was sold with either Atari's color monitor or less expensive monochrome monitor. Color graphics modes are available only on the former while the highest-resolution mode requires the monochrome monitor. Most models can display the color modes on a TV. In Germany and some other markets, the ST gained a foothold for CAD and desktop publishing. With built-in MIDI ports, it was popular for music sequencing and as a controller of musical instruments among amateur and professional musicians. The Atari ST's primary competitor was the Amiga from Commodore.
The 520ST and 1040ST were followed by the Mega series, the STE, and the portable STacy. In the early 1990s, Atari released three final evolutions of the ST with significant technical differences from the original models: TT030 (1990), Mega STE (1991), and Falcon (1992). Atari discontinued the entire ST computer line in 1993, shifting the company's focus to the Jaguar video game console.

entries.title: We Are the World
entries.summary: We Are the World brought American recording stars together as USA for Africa to support famine relief. Written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie, the charity single turned a shared recording session into an international fundraising project.
body:
We Are the World was USA for Africa's 1985 charity single, written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie and produced by Quincy Jones for the album of the same name. It raised money in response to Ethiopia's 1983–1985 famine. Reported worldwide sales exceeded 20 million physical copies, placing it among the most widely sold singles.

The project began when musician and activist Harry Belafonte sought an American response to the British-based group Band Aid's Do They Know It's Christmas?, released in 1984. Agent Ken Kragen brought musicians together. Jackson and Richie worked on the song in January, with revisions continuing during the first recording session on 22 January. The larger session on 28 January united performers including Bruce Springsteen, Cyndi Lauper, Paul Simon, Stevie Wonder and Tina Turner. The single was released on 7 March 1985.
story_headings: Writing and recording a charity single

provenance.full_source_extract:
"We Are the World" is a charity single recorded by the supergroup USA for Africa in 1985. It was written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie and produced by Quincy Jones for the album We Are the World to raise money for the 1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia. With sales in excess of 20 million physical copies, it is the eighth-best-selling single of all time.
After the British group Band Aid released the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" in 1984, the musician and activist Harry Belafonte decided to create an American single for African famine relief. The agent Ken Kragen enlisted several musicians for the project. Jackson and Richie completed the writing the night before the first recording session on January 28, 1985. The recording brought together some of the era's best-known recording artists, including Bruce Springsteen, Cyndi Lauper, Paul Simon, Stevie Wonder, and Tina Turner. 
"We Are the World" was released on March 7, 1985, by Columbia Records. It topped music charts throughout the world, became the fastest-selling US pop single in history and the first single to be certified multi-platinum, and was certified quadruple platinum. Its awards include four Grammy Awards, one American Music Award, and a People's Choice Award.
"We Are the World" was promoted with a music video, a VHS, a special edition magazine, a simulcast, and books, posters and shirts. It raised more than $80 million (equivalent to $235 million in 2025) for humanitarian aid in Africa and the United States. Another cast of singers recorded a new version, "We Are the World 25 for Haiti", following the 2010 Haiti earthquake.

entries.title: Studio Ghibli
entries.summary: Studio Ghibli is the Japanese animation studio whose films include My Neighbor Totoro and Spirited Away. Built around the work of Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata, it also produced shorts, advertising and films for television.
body:
Studio Ghibli opened on 15 June 1985, bringing together directors Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata with producer Toshio Suzuki, under publisher Tokuma Shoten. Its beginnings drew on people from Topcraft; the studio later established its base in Koganei, Tokyo. Beyond its feature films, Ghibli produced short works, television commercials and two television films. Its productions have won awards and earned recognition from critics and audiences.

Totoro, the large spirit in My Neighbor Totoro (1988), became the studio's mascot and best-known character. His appearance recalls both tanuki, or raccoon dogs, and cats. Among Ghibli's biggest box-office successes are Princess Mononoke (1997), Spirited Away (2001), Howl's Moving Castle (2004), Ponyo (2008) and The Boy and the Heron (2023).

Studio Ghibli Inc. (Japanese: 株式会社スタジオジブリ, Hepburn: Kabushiki-gaisha Sutajio Jiburi) is a Japanese animation studio based in Koganei, Tokyo. It was founded on June 15, 1985, by directors Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata and producer Toshio Suzuki, after acquiring Topcraft's assets. It has a strong presence in the animation industry and has expanded its portfolio to include various media such as short subjects, television commercials and two television films. The studio's work is highly acclaimed by both critics and audiences and has been recognized with numerous awards. Their mascot and most recognizable character is Totoro from the 1988 film My Neighbor Totoro, a giant spirit inspired by raccoon dogs (tanuki) and cats (neko). Among the studio's highest-grossing films are Princess Mononoke (1997), Spirited Away (2001), Howl's Moving Castle (2004), Ponyo (2008), and The Boy and the Heron (2023).
Studio Ghibli's major awards across organizations include two Academy Awards for Best Animated Feature, one Golden Globe Award for Best Animated Feature Film, one BAFTA Award for Best Animated Film, one Golden Bear, three Animage Grand Prix awards and six Japan Academy Prizes. Four of the studio's films are among the ten highest-grossing Japanese feature films; Spirited Away is fourth, grossing ¥31.68 billion in Japan and over US$380 million worldwide. In 2026 the Studio Ghibli was awarded the Princess of Asturias Award in the category of "Communication and Humanities".

entries.title: Back to the Future
entries.summary: Back to the Future sends Marty McFly into the past, where disrupting his parents' first meeting puts his own existence at risk. The film builds its family comedy around the practical consequences of trying to repair that mistake.
body:
In Back to the Future, teenager Marty McFly travels from 1985 to 1955 in a DeLorean time machine. By interrupting his parents' first meeting, he endangers his own future. He must bring them together while finding a way home with scientist Emmett Brown.

Robert Zemeckis directed the film from a screenplay he wrote with Bob Gale. They developed the idea in 1980, then faced repeated studio rejections before Universal backed it. Michael J. Fox ultimately played Marty in the film, which opened in American cinemas on 3 July 1985. The family comedy unfolds through the problems his journey into the past has created.
story_headings: Marty has to put his parents' future back together

provenance.full_source_extract:
Back to the Future is a 1985 American science fiction film directed by Robert Zemeckis and written by Zemeckis and Bob Gale. It stars Michael J. Fox, Christopher Lloyd, Lea Thompson, Crispin Glover, and Thomas F. Wilson. Set in 1985, it follows Marty McFly (Fox), a teenager accidentally sent back to 1955 in a time-traveling DeLorean automobile built by his eccentric scientist friend Emmett "Doc" Brown (Lloyd), where he inadvertently prevents his future parents from falling in love – threatening his own existence – and is forced to reconcile them and somehow get back to the future.
Gale and Zemeckis conceived the idea for Back to the Future in 1980. They were desperate for a successful film after numerous collaborative failures, but the project was rejected more than forty times by various studios because it was not considered raunchy enough to compete with the successful comedies of the era. A development deal was secured with Universal Pictures following Zemeckis's success directing Romancing the Stone (1984). Fox was the first choice to portray Marty but was unavailable; Eric Stoltz was cast instead. Shortly after principal photography began in November 1984, Zemeckis determined Stoltz was not right for the part and made the concessions necessary to hire Fox, including re-filming scenes already shot with Stoltz and adding $4 million to the budget. Back to the Future was filmed in and around California and on sets at Universal Studios, and concluded the following April.
After highly successful test screenings, the release date was brought forward to July 3, 1985, giving the film more time in theaters during the busiest period of the theatrical year. The change resulted in a rushed post-production schedule and some incomplete special effects. Nevertheless, Back to the Future was a critical and commercial success, earning $381.1 million to become the highest-grossing film of 1985 worldwide. Critics praised the story, humor, and the cast, particularly Fox, Lloyd, Thompson, and Glover. It received multiple award nominations and won an Academy Award, three Saturn Awards, and a Hugo Award. Its theme song, "The Power of Love" by Huey Lewis and the News, was also a success.
Back to the Future has since grown in esteem and is now considered by critics and audiences to be one of the greatest science fiction films and among the best films ever made. In 2007, the United States Library of Congress selected it for preservation in the National Film Registry. The film was followed by two sequels, Back to the Future Part II (1989) and Back to the Future Part III (1990). Spurred by the film's dedicated fan following and effect on popular culture, Universal Studios launched a multimedia franchise, which now includes video games, theme park rides, an animated television series, and a stage musical. Its enduring popularity has prompted numerous books about its production, documentaries, and commercials.

entries.title: Live Aid
entries.summary: Live Aid linked concerts in London and Philadelphia to raise money for famine relief in Ethiopia. Satellite broadcasting carried the performances across the world, extending the fundraising movement begun by Band Aid's charity single.
body:
Live Aid took place on Saturday, 13 July 1985, at Wembley Stadium in London and John F. Kennedy Stadium in Philadelphia. Bob Geldof and Midge Ure organised the two-venue benefit to raise further funds for people affected by Ethiopia's 1983–1985 famine. It followed the success of Band Aid's Do They Know It's Christmas?, released in December 1984, and was promoted as a global jukebox.

Concerts inspired by the initiative also took place that day in the Soviet Union, Canada, Japan, Yugoslavia, Austria, Australia and West Germany. The satellite links made Live Aid a television event on an exceptional scale. Audience estimates vary: the British Music Experience's exhibition drawn from Geldof's archive cites the upper estimate of 1.9 billion viewers across more than 150 countries, roughly 40 per cent of the world's population at the time.
story_headings: Two stadiums connected to a worldwide audience

provenance.full_source_extract:
Live Aid was a two-venue benefit concert and music-based fund-raising initiative held on Saturday, 13 July 1985. The event was organised by Bob Geldof and Midge Ure to raise further funds for relief of the 1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia, a movement that started with the release of the successful charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" in December 1984. Billed as the "global jukebox", Live Aid was held simultaneously at Wembley Stadium in London and John F. Kennedy Stadium in Philadelphia.
On the same day, concerts inspired by the initiative were held in other countries, such as the Soviet Union, Canada, Japan, Yugoslavia, Austria, Australia, and West Germany. It was one of the largest satellite link-ups and television broadcasts of all time. An estimated audience of 1.9 billion people in 150 nations watched the live broadcast, nearly 40 percent of the world population.
The impact of Live Aid on famine relief has been debated for years. One aid relief worker stated that following the publicity generated by the concert, "humanitarian concern is now at the centre of foreign policy" for Western governments. Geldof has said: "We took an issue that was nowhere on the political agenda and, through the lingua franca of the planet – which is not English but rock 'n' roll – we were able to address the intellectual absurdity and the moral repulsion of people dying of want in a world of surplus." In another interview he stated that Live Aid "created something permanent and self-sustaining" but also asked why Africa was getting poorer.
The organisers of Live Aid tried to run aid efforts directly, channelling millions of pounds to NGOs in Ethiopia. It has been alleged that much of this went to the Ethiopian government of Mengistu Haile Mariam – a regime the UK prime minister Margaret Thatcher opposed – and it is also alleged some funds were spent on guns. Although the BBC World Service programme Assignment reported in March 2010 that the funds had been diverted, the BBC Editorial Complaints Unit later found "that there was no evidence to support such statements". Brian Barder, British Ambassador to Ethiopia from 1982 to 1986, wrote on his website: "The programme itself, and in particular the BBC's advance publicity for it, gave the impression that these allegations concerned not only the aid operation in TPLF [rebel]-controlled areas but also the much larger international relief aid operation in the rest of Ethiopia, including in particular money for famine relief raised by Bob Geldof's Band Aid and Live Aid. This impression is entirely false. Nothing of the sort occurred."

entries.title: Amiga 1000
entries.summary: Commodore's first Amiga combined a Motorola 68000 with dedicated graphics and sound hardware and an operating system able to share processing time between tasks. Additional memory could be fitted through an expansion module and an external connector.
body:
The Amiga 1000, or A1000, was the first computer in Commodore International's Amiga range. Presented on 23 July 1985, it reached the market later that year. Its 16/32-bit Motorola 68000 worked alongside graphics and sound hardware that made the machine technically ambitious for its time. A preemptive multitasking operating system divided processing time between running tasks.

The A1000 loaded Kickstart, the core system software, from disk into 256 KB of dedicated memory, which was then protected against further writes. Separately, it shipped with 256 KB of working RAM. Commodore's 256 KB expansion doubled that to 512 KB, and the external expansion connector allowed a total of up to 8.5 MB.
story_headings: Multitasking and expandable memory

entries.title: Rita Levi-Montalcini wins the Nobel Prize
entries.summary: Italian neurobiologist Rita Levi-Montalcini shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on growth factors. The award recognised discoveries that included nerve growth factor, central to her research.
body:
Rita Levi-Montalcini, the Italian neurobiologist born on 22 April 1909, shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Stanley Cohen for their discoveries of growth factors. Her work on nerve growth factor formed part of the research recognised by the award.

In 2001, her contribution to science earned her appointment as an Italian senator for life, a position she held until her death in 2012. On 22 April 2009 she became the first Nobel laureate to turn one hundred, with celebrations at Rome's City Hall.

entries.title: Chernobyl disaster
entries.summary: The Chernobyl disaster began when reactor 4 exploded during a test in Soviet Ukraine. Radioactive material escaped into the environment, requiring a vast emergency response and leaving an exclusion zone with lasting consequences for people and the land.
body:
Reactor 4 at the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded on 26 April 1986, near Pripyat in Soviet Ukraine. Operators were testing how cooling would be maintained during a power failure. After an unintended fall in reactor output, the test proceeded under unstable low-power conditions; design flaws contributed to a sudden power surge during shutdown.

The accident released large quantities of radioactive material. Dozens of plant and emergency workers died from injuries and acute radiation effects, and a lasting exclusion zone was established. More than 500,000 people took part in the response and cleanup. Classified at the highest level of the International Nuclear Event Scale, the disaster left extensive environmental and health consequences.
story_headings: A low-power test ends in disaster

provenance.date_note: The requested work/event and its year correspond to the independently reviewed source passage. Exact day/month should only be added when explicitly documented.
provenance.full_source_extract:
On 26 April 1986, reactor 4 of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, located near Pripyat in the Ukrainian SSR of the Soviet Union, exploded. The accident resulted in dozens of direct deaths and a major release of radioactive material into the environment, causing widespread health effects and requiring the establishment of the Chernobyl exclusion zone. The response involved more than 500,000 personnel and cost an estimated 18 billion rubles (about $85 billion in 2026). It remains the most destructive nuclear disaster and the most expensive disaster in history, with an estimated cost of US$700 billion. It is one of only two nuclear accidents rated at the maximum severity on the International Nuclear Event Scale, the other being the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident in Japan.
The disaster occurred while conducting a test to simulate the cooling of the reactor during a serious accident in blackout conditions. The operators carried out the test following an accidental drop in reactor power. Upon shutting down the reactor in such conditions, pervasive design flaws led to a power surge. The reactor components ruptured and lost coolant, and the resulting steam explosions and meltdown destroyed the reactor building. This was followed by a meltdown and fire that dispersed radioactive contaminants across the Soviet Union and Europe. The Soviet government established an exclusion zone with a 10-kilometre (6.2 mi) radius 36 hours after the accident, initially evacuating around 49,000 people. This was later expanded to 30 kilometres (19 mi), resulting in the evacuation of approximately 68,000 more people. The government did not publicly acknowledge the disaster until two days after the explosion, when elevated radiation levels were detected in Sweden.
Following the explosion, which killed two engineers and severely burned two others, an emergency operation began to put out the fires and stabilize the reactor. Of the 237 workers hospitalized, 134 showed symptoms of acute radiation syndrome (ARS); 28 of them died within three months. Over the next decade, 14 more workers (nine of whom had ARS) died of various causes mostly unrelated to radiation exposure. This is the only instance in commercial nuclear power history where radiation-related fatalities occurred. As of 2005, 6000 cases of childhood thyroid cancer occurred within the affected populations (15 of them fatal), "a large fraction" being attributed to the accident. Long-term death estimates range from up to 4,000 in Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia (per the United Nations) to 16,000 in total across Europe.
Pripyat was abandoned and replaced by the purpose-built city of Slavutych. The Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant sarcophagus, completed in December 1986, reduced the spread of radioactive contamination and provided radiological protection for the crews of the undamaged reactors. In 2016–2018, the Chernobyl New Safe Confinement was constructed around the old sarcophagus to enable the removal of the reactor debris, and clean-up is scheduled for completion by 2065.

entries.title: Watchmen #1
entries.summary: Watchmen imagines an America whose history has been altered by costumed heroes, with war against the Soviet Union drawing closer. Its twelve-part story examines the power, political loyalties and compromises behind the superhero role.
body: The first issue of Watchmen went on sale on 13 May 1986, beginning DC's twelve-part series written by Alan Moore, drawn by Dave Gibbons and coloured by John Higgins. Its America has been changed by costumed heroes and now faces the possibility of war with the Soviet Union. Most vigilantes have retired, been outlawed or entered government service. Moore initially proposed using characters DC had acquired from Charlton Comics, but creating new ones gave the team freedom to determine their fates. Through their powers, compromises and political roles, the series brings the anxieties of its time into the superhero story.

provenance.full_source_extract:
Watchmen is a comic book limited series created by the British creative team of writer Alan Moore, artist Dave Gibbons, and colorist John Higgins. It was published monthly by DC Comics in 1986 and 1987 before being collected in a single-volume edition in 1987. Watchmen originated from a story proposal Moore submitted to DC featuring superhero characters that the company had acquired from Charlton Comics. As Moore's proposed story would have left many of the characters unusable for future stories, managing editor Dick Giordano convinced Moore to create original characters instead.
Moore used the story as a means of reflecting contemporary anxieties, deconstructing and satirizing the superhero concept, and making political commentary. Watchmen depicts an alternative history in which superheroes emerged in the 1940s and 1960s and their presence changed history so that the United States won the Vietnam War and the Watergate scandal was never exposed. In 1985, the country is edging toward World War III with the Soviet Union, freelance costumed vigilantes have been outlawed and most former superheroes are in retirement or working for the government. The story focuses on the protagonists' personal development and moral struggles as an investigation into the murder of a government-sponsored superhero pulls them out of retirement.
Watchmen uses a nine-panel grid layout throughout the series and incorporates recurring symbols such as a blood-stained smiley face. All but the last issue feature supplemental fictional documents that add to the series' backstory and the narrative is intertwined with that of another story, an in-story pirate comic titled Tales of the Black Freighter, which one of the characters reads. Structured at times as a nonlinear narrative, the story skips through space, time, and plot. In the same manner, entire scenes and dialogues have parallels with others through synchronicity, coincidence, and repeated imagery.
A commercial success, Watchmen has received critical acclaim both in the comics and mainstream press. Watchmen was recognized in Time's  "List of the 100 Best Novels" as one of the best English language novels published since 1923. In a retrospective review, the BBC's Nicholas Barber described it as "the moment comic books grew up". Moore opposed this idea, stating, "I tend to think that, no, comics hadn't grown up. There were a few titles that were more adult than people were used to. But the majority of comics titles were pretty much the same as they'd ever been. It wasn't comics growing up. I think it was more comics meeting the emotional age of the audience coming the other way."
After several attempts to adapt the series into a feature film, director Zack Snyder's Watchmen was released in 2009. An episodic video game, Watchmen: The End Is Nigh, was released to coincide with the film's release. DC Comics published Before Watchmen, a series of nine prequel miniseries, in 2012, and Doomsday Clock, a 12-issue limited series and sequel to the original Watchmen series, from 2017 to 2019 – both without Moore's or Gibbons' involvement. The second series integrated the Watchmen characters within the DC Universe. A standalone sequel, Rorschach by Tom King, was published between October 2020 and September 2021. A television continuation to the original comic, set 34 years after the comic's timeline, was broadcast on HBO from October to December 2019 with Gibbons' involvement. Moore has expressed his displeasure with adaptations and sequels of Watchmen and asked for his name not to be used for future works.

entries.title: The Joshua Tree
entries.summary: The Joshua Tree brings American and Irish roots music into U2's songwriting, with spiritual imagery alongside political unease. Personal losses and experiences abroad shape an album drawn to America's mythology and troubled by its realities.
body: Released on 9 March 1987, The Joshua Tree was produced by Daniel Lanois and Brian Eno. U2 drew on American and Irish roots music, building direct song structures around spiritual imagery and political concerns. Their experiences in the United States brought admiration for the country's mythology into contact with unease about its realities. Recording in houses in Ireland gave the sessions a relaxed atmosphere, while events beyond them entered the lyrics: Amnesty International benefit concerts, Bono's travels in Central America and the death of the band's roadie Greg Carroll. Public events and personal grief consequently meet across the record.
story_headings: U2's encounters with America

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Joshua Tree is the fifth studio album by the Irish rock band U2. It was produced by Daniel Lanois and Brian Eno, and was released on 9 March 1987 by Island Records. In contrast to the ambient experimentation of their 1984 album The Unforgettable Fire, for The Joshua Tree the band aimed for a harder-hitting sound within the limitation of conventional song structures. The album is influenced by American and Irish roots music, and through sociopolitically conscious lyrics embellished with spiritual imagery, it contrasts the group's antipathy for the "real America" with their fascination with the "mythical America". The record's theme was inspired by their experiences in the United States, as well as American literature and politics.
Recording began in January 1986 in Ireland, and to foster a relaxed, creative atmosphere, the group primarily recorded in two houses. Several events during the sessions helped shape the conscious tone of the album, including the band's participation in the Conspiracy of Hope benefit concerts for Amnesty International, the death of their roadie Greg Carroll, and lead vocalist Bono's travels to Central America. Recording was completed in November 1986; additional production continued into January 1987. U2 sought a "cinematic" quality that would evoke a sense of location, in particular, the open spaces of the U.S. They represented this in the sleeve photography depicting them in American desert landscapes.
The Joshua Tree received critical acclaim, increasing U2's stature significantly. It topped the charts in over 20 countries −  including the U.S., marking the group's first number one there. It produced the hit singles "With or Without You", "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For", and "Where the Streets Have No Name", the first two of which became the group's only number-one singles in the U.S. The Joshua Tree won Grammy Awards for Album of the Year and Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal at the 1988 ceremony. The Joshua Tree Tour was the highest-grossing North American tour of 1987 and marked U2's first time performing in stadiums.  
Frequently listed among the greatest albums of all time, The Joshua Tree is one of the world's best-selling albums as well as U2's best-selling album, with over 25 million copies sold, including a diamond certification in the U.S. U2 commemorated the record's 20th anniversary with a remastered re-release, and its 30th anniversary with concert tours and a reissue. In 2014, The Joshua Tree was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, and was selected for preservation in the U.S. National Recording Registry, having been deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the Library of Congress.

entries.title: European operators agree on GSM
entries.summary: A shared digital mobile network was the goal of the agreement European operators signed in September 1987. Cooperation over GSM would support compatible equipment, international roaming and, later, data services alongside voice calls.
body:
In September 1987, fifteen operators from thirteen countries committed to developing and deploying GSM, a common digital cellular system. Their memorandum of understanding, signed in Copenhagen, helped establish a shared market for networks and compatible equipment.

GSM initially concentrated on digital voice calls using time-division multiple access, or TDMA. Later extensions introduced data services through GPRS and EDGE. Compatibility between national networks also made international roaming possible, allowing subscribers to use their phones outside their home country.
story_headings: A common standard across national borders

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) is a family of standards to describe the protocols for second-generation (2G) digital cellular networks, as used by mobile devices such as mobile phones and mobile broadband modems. GSM is also a trademark owned by the GSM Association. "GSM" may also refer to the voice codec initially used in GSM.

2G networks were developed as a replacement for first generation (1G) analog cellular networks. The original GSM standard, which was developed by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI), originally described a digital, circuit-switched network optimized for full duplex voice telephony, employing time division multiple access (TDMA) between stations. This expanded over time to include data communications, first by circuit-switched transport, then by packet data transport via its upgraded standards, GPRS and then EDGE. GSM exists in various versions based on the frequency bands used.
GSM was first implemented in Finland in December 1991. It became the global standard for mobile cellular communications, with over 2 billion GSM subscribers globally in 2006, far above its competing standard, CDMA. Its share reached over 90% market share by the mid-2010s, and operating in over 219 countries and territories. The specifications and maintenance of GSM passed over to the 3GPP body in 2000, which at the time developed third-generation (3G) UMTS standards, followed by the fourth-generation (4G) LTE Advanced and the fifth-generation 5G standards, which do not form part of the GSM standard. Beginning in the late 2010s, various carriers worldwide started to shut down their GSM networks; nevertheless, as a result of the network's widespread use, the acronym "GSM" is still used as a generic term for the plethora of G mobile phone technologies evolved from it or mobile phones itself.

The decision to develop a continental standard eventually resulted in a unified, open, standard-based network which was larger than that in the United States.

entries.title: The Last Emperor
entries.subtitle: Puyi's power and dependence behind the palace walls
entries.summary: The Last Emperor follows China's Puyi from childhood enthronement through political upheaval and imprisonment. Bernardo Bertolucci's historical epic traces the gap between the authority attached to his title and the restrictions governing his life.
body: Bernardo Bertolucci's The Last Emperor follows Puyi from his enthronement as a child in 1908 through the upheavals that bring imperial rule in China to an end. John Lone plays the adult Puyi, alongside an international cast that includes Joan Chen and Peter O'Toole. Released in Italy on 23 October 1987, the historical epic examines both his official authority and his continual dependence on others.

Inside the Forbidden City, court rituals confer extraordinary status on the child emperor while limiting what he can see and do. As Puyi grows up, the world outside changes faster than the court. His later efforts to recover authority make him useful to other political interests. The film repeatedly returns to his imprisonment and interrogation, setting different stages of his life against the explanations he has learned to give for his choices.

Vittorio Storaro's cinematography and Ferdinando Scarfiotti's production design distinguish the palace's enclosed splendour from the places Puyi inhabits later. Crowds bowing before a child and restrictions imposed on the adult ruler reveal the different forms that control takes throughout his life. Music by Ryuichi Sakamoto, David Byrne and Cong Su accompanies these shifts in atmosphere. The film won all nine Academy Awards for which it was nominated, including Best Picture and Best Director for Bertolucci.

entries.title: My Neighbor Totoro
entries.summary: My Neighbor Totoro follows two sisters who encounter friendly forest spirits after moving to rural Japan. Hayao Miyazaki's animated fantasy approaches childhood and country life through an attention to nature shaped by animism and Shinto imagery.
body:
My Neighbor Totoro is an animated fantasy written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki, made by Studio Ghibli for Tokuma Shoten and released in Japan on 16 April 1988. Two young sisters move to the countryside with their father in postwar Japan and meet friendly forest spirits. The Japanese voice cast includes Noriko Hidaka, Chika Sakamoto and Hitoshi Takagi.

Their encounters bring together childhood, the pleasures of rural life and concern for the environment, with animist ideas and Shinto imagery. The film won critical acclaim internationally and eventually took more than $41 million at cinemas worldwide; home video and merchandise generated considerably greater revenue.

Recognition for the 1988 film included Animage's Anime Grand Prix, the Mainichi Film Award, first place in Kinema Junpo's Japanese film ranking and the Blue Ribbon Special Award.
story_headings: Two sisters and the spirits of the countryside

provenance.full_source_extract:
My Neighbor Totoro is a 1988 Japanese animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki and animated by Studio Ghibli for Tokuma Shoten. It stars the voices of Noriko Hidaka, Chika Sakamoto and Hitoshi Takagi, and focuses on two young sisters who, after moving with their father to the countryside, experience interactions with friendly wood spirits in postwar Japan.
The film explores themes such as animism, Shinto symbology, environmentalism, childhood and the joys of rural living. My Neighbor Totoro received worldwide critical acclaim, and grossed over $41 million worldwide at the box office; the film also grossed significantly more from home video sales and merchandise.
My Neighbor Totoro received numerous awards, including the Animage Anime Grand Prix prize, the Mainichi Film Award, and Kinema Junpo Award for Best Film in 1988. It also received the Special Award at the Blue Ribbon Awards in the same year. The film is widely regarded as one of the greatest animated films of all time, ranking 41st in Empire magazine's "The 100 Best Films of World Cinema" in 2010 and the number-one animated film on the 2012 Sight & Sound critics' poll of all-time greatest films. The film and its titular character have become cultural icons, and made multiple cameo appearances in other films. Totoro also serves as the mascot for Studio Ghibli and is recognized as one of the most popular characters in Japanese animation.

entries.title: Akira
entries.summary: Akira follows two childhood friends from a biker gang into a military crisis in the futuristic city of Neo-Tokyo. Katsuhiro Otomo's animated cyberpunk thriller adapts his manga around Tetsuo's emerging telekinetic powers and their destructive consequences.
body:
Akira is Katsuhiro Otomo's Japanese animated cyberpunk action thriller, released on 16 July 1988. Produced by Ryōhei Suzuki and Shunzō Katō, it was written by Otomo and Izo Hashimoto from Otomo's manga, which began in 1982. In the dystopian Neo-Tokyo of 2019, biker gang leader Shōtarō Kaneda's childhood friend Tetsuo Shima develops powerful telekinetic abilities after a motorcycle accident involving a psychic child. His powers eventually threaten an entire military complex.

The film carries over much of the manga's character design and settings, but follows a substantially different plot, leaving out much of its latter half. The manga continued for another two years after the film appeared. Shōji Yamashiro composed the score, performed by Geinoh Yamashirogumi, drawing extensively on Indonesian gamelan and Japanese noh music.

provenance.full_source_extract:
Akira (Japanese: アキラ, pronounced [ä́.k̟ʲì.ɾä̀]) is a 1988 Japanese animated cyberpunk action thriller film directed by Katsuhiro Otomo, produced by Ryōhei Suzuki and Shunzō Katō, and written by Otomo and Izo Hashimoto, based on Otomo's 1982 manga Akira. Set in a dystopian 2019, it follows Shōtarō Kaneda, the leader of a biker gang whose childhood friend, Tetsuo Shima, acquires powerful telekinetic abilities after colliding with a child esper in a motorcycle accident, eventually threatening an entire military complex in the sprawling futuristic metropolis of Neo-Tokyo.
While most of the character designs and settings were adapted from the manga, the plot differs considerably and does not include much of the latter half of the manga, which continued publication for two years after the film's release. The soundtrack, which draws heavily from traditional Indonesian gamelan and Japanese noh music, was composed by Shōji Yamashiro and performed by Geinoh Yamashirogumi.
Akira was released in Japan on July 16, 1988, by Toho; it was released the following year in the United States by Streamline Pictures. It garnered an international cult following after various theatrical and VHS releases, eventually earning over $80 million worldwide in home video sales. A landmark in Japanese animation, the film is widely cited as an influential work in the development of anime, adult animation, and Japanese cyberpunk. The film had a massive impact on popular culture worldwide, paving the way for the growth of anime and Japanese popular culture in the Western world, as well as influencing numerous works in animation, comics, film, music, television, and video games.

entries.title: Cinema Paradiso
entries.subtitle: A boy discovers cinema from the projection booth
entries.summary: Cinema Paradiso follows a director remembering the projectionist who introduced him to film as a child. In Giuseppe Tornatore's Sicilian town, the picture house brings together a friendship, a working craft and the life of its audience.
body: Giuseppe Tornatore's Cinema Paradiso centres on Salvatore, a successful director remembering his childhood friendship with a cinema projectionist. Released in Italy on 17 November 1988 as Nuovo Cinema Paradiso, it places their friendship in a Sicilian town's picture house. Philippe Noiret plays Alfredo, whose daily work introduces the boy to both the machinery and the pleasures of film.

Young Totò is fascinated by the projection booth, where reels, light and a hazardous machine produce images for a packed auditorium. Alfredo teaches him the practical work with a mixture of impatience and affection. Downstairs, spectators laugh, argue and return to their familiar seats, making the audience part of the spectacle. The local priest orders kisses to be cut before a film can be shown. What the town watches together depends on decisions made by the people who control its cinema.

Salvatore's return as an adult brings the cinema building, his friendship with Alfredo and his departure from the town into the same recollection. Ennio Morricone's score, which also includes music by Andrea Morricone, connects these passages through time. The final gift draws together the physical work of handling film and the feelings preserved in its images. The Cannes Grand Prix and the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film helped bring this story of a small local cinema to international audiences.

The booth, the audience and the censor
What survives in a reel of film

entries.title: Tiananmen Square protests and massacre
entries.summary: Demonstrations in Beijing during spring 1989 brought demands for political participation together with anger over corruption and inflation. After weeks of protest and failed negotiations, the government used military force to suppress the movement.
body: Students and workers began gathering in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in April 1989 after the death of Hu Yaobang, a Communist Party leader associated with reform. During rapid economic change, their demands expressed concern about corruption, inflation and limits on political participation. Weeks of demonstrations and unsuccessful negotiations followed. The government declared martial law on 20 May. On the night of 3–4 June, troops used lethal force as they advanced through central Beijing to occupy the square and suppress the movement. The protests and massacre became known internationally by the name Tiananmen, and in China as the June Fourth Incident.
story_headings: From public mourning to military repression

provenance.date_note: The requested work/event and its year correspond to the independently reviewed source passage. Exact day/month should only be added when explicitly documented.
provenance.full_source_extract:
Protests led by students and workers, known in China as the June Fourth Incident, were held in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, China, from 15 April to 4 June 1989. After weeks of unsuccessful attempts between the demonstrators and the Chinese government to find a peaceful resolution, the Chinese government initiated martial law in late May and deployed troops to occupy the square on the night of 3 June in what is referred to as the Tiananmen Square massacre. The events are sometimes called the '89 Democracy Movement, the Tiananmen Square Incident, or the Tiananmen uprising. The Chinese government terms the events the political turmoil between the spring and summer of 1989.
The protests were initiated by the death of former pro-reform Chinese Communist Party (CCP) general secretary Hu Yaobang in April 1989, amid the backdrop of rapid economic development and social change in post-Mao China. The movement's goals reflected anxieties among the people and political elite about the nation's future. Common grievances at the time included inflation, corruption, dismantling of the "iron rice bowl", limited preparedness of graduates for the new economy, and restrictions on political participation. Although the protests were highly disorganised with varying goals, student protestors called for reforms including the rollback of the removal of iron rice bowl jobs, greater political accountability, constitutional due process, democracy, freedom of the press, and freedom of speech. Workers' protests were generally focused on economic issues, specifically inflation and Deng's economic reforms, which weakened Mao-era guarantees such as lifetime employment in state-owned enterprises and associated workplace benefits. These groups united around anti-corruption demands, adjusting economic policies, and protecting social security. At the height of the protests on May 17, about one million people were assembled in the square.
As the protests developed, Chinese authorities responded with both conciliatory and hardline tactics, exposing deep divisions within the party leadership. By May, a student-led hunger strike galvanised support around the country for the demonstrators, and the protests spread to some 400 cities.
On 20 May, the State Council declared martial law, and as many as 300,000 troops were mobilized to Beijing, but were halted by mass nonviolent resistance from the protestors and Beijing's civilian population. After several weeks of standoffs and confrontations between the army and demonstrators, a 1 June meeting among the CCP's leadership decided to clear the square. Chinese troops advanced into central parts of Beijing through the city's major highways in the early morning hours of 4 June, and engaged in bloody clashes with demonstrators attempting to block them, in which many people – demonstrators, bystanders, and soldiers – were killed or injured. The vast majority of killings were clustered in Beijing's western suburbs along Chang'an Avenue. Estimates of the death toll vary from several hundreds to the low thousands, with thousands more wounded. On June 5, after military forces cleared the Square, an unidentified individual, later referred to as "Tank Man" briefly stood in front of a column of tanks, temporarily blocking their movement. The photograph of the event became widely circulated internationally and is often regarded as one of the most recognizable images of the 20th century. It is subject to censorship in China.
The event had both immediate and longer-term consequences. Western countries imposed arm embargoes on China and various Western media outlets labeled the crackdown a massacre. In the aftermath of the protests, the Chinese government suppressed other protests around China, carried out mass arrests of protesters which catalysed Operation Yellowbird, strictly controlled coverage of the events in the domestic and foreign affiliated press, and demoted or purged officials it deemed sympathetic to the protests. The government also invested heavily into creating more effective police riot control units. More broadly, the suppression was followed by a halt to political reforms which began in 1986 as well as the New Enlightenment movement, and a slowdown in liberalising policies of the 1980s, which were later partly resumed after Deng Xiaoping's southern tour in 1992. In the longer term, political liberalisation was curtailed, while market-oriented economic reforms continued and were accelerated after 1992 under strong state direction led by Deng Xiaoping.
Considered a watershed event, reactions to the protests set limits on political expression in China that have lasted up to the present day. The events remain one of the most sensitive and most widely censored topics in China.

entries.title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade
entries.summary: A search for the Holy Grail becomes a journey with Indiana Jones’s missing father. Harrison Ford and Sean Connery bring an uneasy family partnership into Steven Spielberg’s third adventure.
story_headings: A father and son searching for the Grail
The origins of an adventurer
body: In Steven Spielberg’s third Indiana Jones film, Harrison Ford’s archaeologist discovers that his father has disappeared while researching the Holy Grail. The search takes Indy through Europe in 1938 and into another confrontation with the Nazis. His father, Professor Henry Jones, is played by Sean Connery; once reunited, their different ways of facing danger turn the expedition into a test of their relationship as well as their knowledge.

An opening adventure with River Phoenix as the young Indy shows how some of the adult character’s familiar traits took shape. The rest of the film returns to him as a son: Henry’s scholarly obsessions and Indy’s impatience repeatedly clash, but the journey gives their shared interest in history a more personal purpose. Their exchanges carry the humour through chases by boat, motorcycle and tank.

entries.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
entries.summary: The opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 allowed people to cross the border dividing the city. It marked a decisive moment in East Germany's Peaceful Revolution and the collapse of communist rule in Central and Eastern Europe.
body: On 9 November 1989, East Berlin's travel restrictions collapsed during East Germany's Peaceful Revolution, opening the border through the Berlin Wall. Sections were breached, while planned demolition began in June 1990. The opening became a decisive stage in the dismantling of the Iron Curtain and formed part of the wider fall of communist regimes in Central and Eastern Europe. Crossings along the inner German border opened soon afterwards. The Malta Summit in early December marked a further step away from Cold War confrontation, and Germany reunified in October 1990.

entries.title: Twin Peaks
entries.subtitle: A murder investigation enters a town's private lives
entries.summary: Twin Peaks begins with a murder investigation that draws an outsider into the private lives of a small town. Its mystery unfolds through dreams, everyday conversations and uneasy shifts between affectionate comedy, melodrama and fear.
body: Created by David Lynch and Mark Frost, Twin Peaks opens with the discovery of Laura Palmer's body in a small town in the northwestern United States. Kyle MacLachlan plays FBI agent Dale Cooper, whose arrival introduces a different approach to the local police investigation. First broadcast on ABC on 8 April 1990, the series connects the murder mystery to the private lives of the people surrounding it.

Cooper's curiosity extends beyond conventional evidence to dreams, intuition and details that might otherwise pass unnoticed. Conversations in diners, homes and workplaces gradually reveal conflicting accounts of Laura's life. Familiar routines make the disturbances harder to dismiss: coffee, pie and affectionate eccentricity coexist with exploitation and fear. Someone who initially seems a comic figure may later emerge in a much darker role.

Angelo Badalamenti's music connects the series' changes of mood, moving between warmth, melancholy and threat. Lynch and Frost give romances and local schemes time alongside the continuing investigation. Television melodrama sits with images and rhythms whose meanings remain elusive. As the episodes aired each week, viewers could discuss their uncertainty together. The original two seasons established a world that Lynch and Frost would revisit in later work.

entries.title: Hubble Space Telescope
entries.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope observes the universe from above Earth's atmosphere, capturing details that atmospheric distortion can obscure from the ground. Its images and measurements have contributed to major developments in astrophysics, including work on the universe's expansion.
body:
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into low Earth orbit on 24 April 1990 and remains in operation. Named after astronomer Edwin Hubble, it is one of NASA's Great Observatories. The Space Telescope Science Institute coordinates the selection of observing targets and processes the data, while the Goddard Space Flight Center controls the spacecraft.

Hubble uses a 2.4-metre mirror and five main working instrument systems, including its fine guidance sensors. Its observations cover ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. Above the atmospheric distortion that affects ground-based telescopes, it can resolve fine details in distant objects. Those observations have supported major advances in astrophysics, including measurements of how quickly the universe is expanding.
story_headings: An observatory above the atmosphere

provenance.full_source_extract:
The Hubble Space Telescope (HST or Hubble) is a space telescope that was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation. It was not the first space telescope, but it is one of the largest and most versatile, renowned as a vital research tool and as a public relations boon for astronomy. The Hubble Space Telescope is named after astronomer Edwin Hubble and is one of NASA's Great Observatories. The Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI) selects Hubble's targets and processes the resulting data, while the Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) controls the spacecraft.
Hubble features a 2.4 m (7 ft 10 in) mirror, and its five main instruments observe in the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. Hubble's orbit outside the distortion of Earth's atmosphere allows it to capture extremely high-resolution images with substantially lower background light than ground-based telescopes. It has recorded some of the most detailed visible light images, allowing a deep view into space. Many Hubble observations have led to breakthroughs in astrophysics, such as determining the rate of expansion of the universe. The Hubble Space Telescope was funded and built in the 1970s by NASA with contributions from the European Space Agency. Its intended launch was in 1983, but the project was beset by technical delays, budget problems, and the 1986 Challenger disaster. 
Hubble was launched on STS-31 in 1990, but its main mirror had been ground incorrectly, resulting in spherical aberration that compromised the telescope's capabilities. The optics were corrected to their intended quality by a servicing mission, STS-61, in 1993. Hubble is the only telescope designed to be maintained in space by astronauts. Five Space Shuttle missions repaired, upgraded, and replaced systems on the telescope, including all five of the main instruments. The fifth mission was initially canceled on safety grounds following the Columbia disaster (2003), but after NASA administrator Michael D. Griffin approved it, the servicing mission was completed in 2009. Hubble completed 30 years of operation in April 2020 and is predicted to last until 2030 to 2040.
Hubble is the visible light telescope in NASA's Great Observatories program; other parts of the spectrum are covered by the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the Spitzer Space Telescope (which covers the infrared bands). The mid-IR-to-visible band successors to the Hubble telescope are the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which was launched on December 25, 2021, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope which was launched on August 30, 2026.

entries.title: Gulf War
entries.summary: The Gulf War followed Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990. An international coalition led by the United States first assembled forces in the region, then launched the air and ground campaign that drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait.
body:
Iraq invaded neighbouring Kuwait on 2 August 1990 under Saddam Hussein. The Gulf War that followed brought Iraq into conflict with a US-led coalition of forty-two countries. Its operations had two phases: Desert Shield, the military buildup from August 1990 to January 1991, and Desert Storm, beginning with air attacks on 17 January. The campaign drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait before the coalition suspended combat on 28 February.

The invasion drew immediate international condemnation. The UN Security Council demanded Iraqi withdrawal and imposed a trade embargo covering Iraq and occupied Kuwait. Meanwhile, coalition forces gathered in the Persian Gulf region. The alliance was the broadest since the Second World War, with the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and Egypt among its largest contributors.
story_headings: From the invasion of Kuwait to Desert Storm

provenance.date_note: The requested work/event and its year correspond to the independently reviewed source passage. Exact day/month should only be added when explicitly documented.
provenance.full_source_extract:
The Gulf War was an armed conflict between Iraq and a 42-country coalition led by the United States in response to Saddam Hussein invading neighboring Kuwait on 2 August 1990. The coalition's efforts were in two phases: Operation Desert Shield, which marked the military buildup from August 1990 to January 1991; and Operation Desert Storm, from the bombing campaign against Iraq on 17 January until the American-led liberation of Kuwait on 28 February.
The invasion of Kuwait was met with immediate international condemnation. The UN Security Council demanded Iraq's immediate withdrawal and imposed a total embargo on products from Iraq and Kuwait. A coalition began a military buildup in the Persian Gulf region. The broadest military alliance since World War II, its largest contributors were the US, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom, and Egypt.
The Security Council issued an ultimatum to Iraq on 29 November 1990, expiring on 15 January 1991, to withdraw from Kuwait, with member-states thereafter empowered to use "all necessary means" to force withdrawal. On 17 January, the coalition began aerial and naval bombardment of Iraq and Kuwait, which continued for five weeks.  Iraq fired missiles at Israel and at Saudi Arabia, but failed to split Muslim-majority countries from the coalition.  On 24 February 1991, the coalition launched a decisive ground assault liberating Kuwait and promptly advancing into Iraqi territory.  The coalition halted its ground advance after one hundred hours, and declared a ceasefire.
In the war's aftermath, the Iraqi government suppressed a series of uprisings until 5 April 1991. Coalition countries responded by establishing two no-fly zones over Iraq's north and south. The United Nations Special Commission sought to end Iraq's weapons of mass destruction programs. In 2003, another US-led coalition invaded and occupied Iraq, beginning the Iraq War.
The conflict's environmental impact included Iraqi forces causing over six hundred oil well fires and the largest oil spill in history until that point. US bombing and demolition of Iraqi chemical weapons facilities were concluded to be the primary cause of Gulf War syndrome, experienced by over 40% of US veterans.

The conflict introduced live news broadcasts from the front lines of the battle, principally by American network CNN.  It earned the nickname "Video Game War", after the daily broadcast of images from cameras onboard American military aircraft. The war highlighted new military technologies including military satellites, precision-guided munitions and a stealth aircraft, the F-117 Nighthawk.  The largest tank battles in American military history were also fought, surpassed only by the Battle of the Bulge: the Battle of Medina Ridge, the Battle of Norfolk, and the Battle of 73 Easting.

entries.title: Dances with Wolves
entries.subtitle: A frontier posting brings an officer into a Lakota community
entries.summary: Dances with Wolves follows a Union officer whose isolated posting brings him into contact with a Lakota community. Patient encounters and attention to language show his relationships developing, as experience changes the assumptions he brought with him.
body: Kevin Costner directs and stars in Dances with Wolves, playing a Union officer stationed alone on the frontier who comes into contact with a Lakota community. Michael Blake adapted the screenplay from his own novel. The film opened in limited release on 9 November 1990. Its extended encounters and careful attention to language give the officer's changing relationships time to develop.

John Dunbar's first encounters with his neighbours involve suspicion, observation and awkward efforts to communicate. Friendship with Kicking Bird and help from Stands With a Fist make further exchanges possible. Visits, shared activities and the buffalo hunt gradually replace his solitary routine. Dunbar writes about what he experiences, so the film follows a change in the way he describes the people around him as well as in his behaviour towards them.

Subtitled Lakota dialogue gives the community conversations that extend beyond its dealings with the newcomer. Dean Semler's landscape photography and John Barry's score provide a broad setting for the unhurried scenes of contact. Dunbar's viewpoint still organises the story. When the United States Army returns, however, he sees the people he has come to know treated according to assumptions he can no longer accept.

entries.title: Mediterraneo
entries.subtitle: Eight soldiers cut off from the war around them
entries.summary: Mediterraneo follows eight Italian soldiers who lose contact with their superiors on a small Greek island during the Second World War. Their lives become intertwined with those of the inhabitants as military routines give way to friendships and personal hopes.
body: Gabriele Salvatores' Mediterraneo sends eight Italian soldiers to a small Greek island during the Second World War. Cut off from their superiors, they gradually share a daily life with the people they were sent to control. Released in Italy on 31 January 1991, the film uses its isolated setting and ensemble of characters to explore the appeal of escaping the roles imposed by war.

The loss of their ship and a broken radio leave the soldiers waiting for orders that never arrive. Patrols and military routines give way to friendships, games, work and romance. Their different temperaments become clearer as each discovers what he wants from this unexpected break. The islanders have needs and lives of their own, making occupation an uneasy form of coexistence. News from outside eventually confronts the men with how far their private refuge has become detached from events elsewhere.

Giancarlo Bigazzi and Marco Falagiani's score gives the island a distinctive sound through acoustic instruments including bouzouki and santur, alongside regional wind and percussion instruments. Recurring themes accompany the passing days as the men grow accustomed to their surroundings. Vincenzo Monteleone's screenplay keeps their relationships at the centre of the story. The 1992 Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film brought international attention to Salvatores' ensemble and its account of escape, belonging and the difficulty of returning.

entries.title: World Wide Web
entries.summary: The World Wide Web connects information through links that readers can follow from one resource to another. Conceived at CERN, it brought browsers, servers and a common page format together for publishing over the Internet.
body: Tim Berners-Lee conceived the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989 as a system for linking information. Its software became available to CERN colleagues in March 1991 and was distributed over the Internet that August. A hyperlink in one document could take a reader directly to another resource. Servers supplied pages to browsers, HTTP governed their exchange and URLs identified their locations. HTML provided a common structure for pages, which came to combine text with images, sound and video as the Web developed. CERN made the software freely usable without royalties in 1993, helping publishing and following links become everyday ways to share information online.

provenance.full_source_extract:
The World Wide Web (also known as WWW, W3, or simply the Web) is a global interconnected information system that enables content sharing over the Internet. It facilitates access to documents and other web resources according to specific rules of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP).
The Web was invented by English computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee while at CERN in 1989 and opened to the public in 1993. It was conceived as a "universal linked information system". Documents and other media content are made available to the network through web servers and can be accessed by programs such as web browsers. Servers and resources on the World Wide Web are identified and located through a character string called a uniform resource locator (URL).
The original and still very common document type is a web page formatted in Hypertext Markup Language (HTML). This markup language supports plain text, images, embedded video and audio contents, and scripts (short programs) that implement complex user interaction. The HTML language also supports hyperlinks (embedded URLs), which provide immediate access to other web resources. Web navigation, or web surfing, is the common practice of following such hyperlinks across multiple websites. Web applications are web pages that function as application software. The information on the Web is transferred across the Internet using HTTP. Multiple web resources with a common theme and usually a common domain name make up a website. A single web server may provide multiple websites, while some websites, especially the most popular ones, may be provided by multiple servers. Website content is provided by a myriad of companies, organisations, government agencies, and individual users; and comprises an enormous amount of educational, entertainment, commercial, and government information.
The World Wide Web has become the world's dominant information systems platform. It is the primary tool that billions of people worldwide use to interact with the Internet.

entries.title: Nevermind
entries.summary: Nevermind brings a more polished sound to Nirvana's mixture of grunge, alternative rock and punk influences. Kurt Cobain's songs combine frustration and social alienation with feminist views, resistance to authority and the strain of personal relationships.
body:
Nirvana's second studio album, Nevermind, was released by DGC Records on 24 September 1991. Producer Butch Vig helped give the American band's music a more polished, radio-friendly sound than its previous work. The main recordings took place in May and June 1991 at Sound City Studios in Van Nuys, California; earlier material came from April 1990 sessions at Smart Studios in Madison, Wisconsin. Howie Weinberg of Masterdisk in New York handled the mastering that August. Nevermind was Nirvana's first album to feature drummer Dave Grohl.

Frontman Kurt Cobain wrote most of the songs, bringing social alienation, frustration, anti-establishment and feminist views, and troubled relationships into the lyrics. Their emotional openness stood apart from much mainstream rock of the period. Grunge and alternative rock form the album's foundations, with acoustic ballads and punk-influenced hard rock extending its range.
story_headings: A clearer sound for Nirvana's songs

provenance.full_source_extract:
Nevermind is the second studio album by American rock band Nirvana, released on September 24, 1991, by DGC Records. Produced by Butch Vig, Nevermind features a more polished, radio-friendly sound than the band's prior work. It was recorded at Sound City Studios in Van Nuys, California, and Smart Studios in Madison, Wisconsin, in May and June 1991, and mastered that August at the Mastering Lab in Hollywood, California. Nevermind was Nirvana's first album to feature drummer Dave Grohl.
Written primarily by frontman Kurt Cobain, the album's lyrical themes include social alienation and frustration, anti-establishment and feminist views, and relationship issues; these were more sensitive compared to what was common in mainstream rock music at the time. Musically rooted in grunge and alternative rock, the album also features acoustic ballads and punk-inspired hard rock. 
Nevermind was an unexpected success, topping the Billboard 200 in January 1992. The lead single, "Smells Like Teen Spirit", reached the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100 was later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. The singles "Come as You Are", "Lithium", and "In Bloom" were also successful. Nevermind was voted the best album of the year in Pazz & Jop critics' poll, while "Smells Like Teen Spirit" also topped the single-of-the-year and video-of-the-year polls. It was nominated for three Grammy Awards, including Best Alternative Music Album.
Nevermind brought Nirvana worldwide fame, with Cobain dubbed by many as the "voice of his generation". The album is generally credited with bringing grunge and alternative rock to a mainstream audience, accelerating the decline of hair metal, and initiating a resurgence of punk culture among the youth of Generation X. Nevermind has sold more than 30 million copies worldwide, making it one of the best-selling albums of all-time. In 2024, it was certified 13 times platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America. Nevermind was added by the Library of Congress to the National Recording Registry in 2004 as "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant", and frequently appears on lists of the greatest albums.

entries.title: Dolby Digital
entries.summary: Dolby Digital compresses multichannel sound for storage and playback, first reaching cinemas through 35mm film prints. Developed by Dolby Laboratories, the technology later spread to broadcasting, recorded video, streaming and game consoles.
body:
Dolby Digital is a family of audio-compression technologies developed by Dolby Laboratories. Introduced commercially in cinemas in 1992 under the name Dolby Stereo Digital, it carried digital sound on 35mm film prints. It subsequently spread to television, satellite radio, streaming services, DVDs, Blu-ray discs and game consoles.

Its original AC-3 codec compresses multichannel audio using the modified discrete cosine transform, or MDCT. This grew from the discrete cosine transform that Nasir Ahmed proposed in 1972 for image compression. In 1987, J. P. Princen, A. W. Johnson and Alan B. Bradley at the University of Surrey developed the modified form underlying this approach to audio coding.

provenance.full_source_extract:
Dolby Digital, originally synonymous with Dolby AC-3 (see below), is the name for a family of audio compression technologies developed by Dolby Laboratories. Called Dolby Stereo Digital until 1995, it uses lossy compression (except for Dolby TrueHD). The first use of Dolby Digital was to provide digital sound in cinemas from 35 mm film prints. It has since also been used for TV broadcast, radio broadcast via satellite, digital video streaming, DVDs, Blu-ray discs and game consoles.
Dolby AC-3 was the original version of the Dolby Digital codec. The basis of the Dolby AC-3 multi-channel audio coding standard is the modified discrete cosine transform (MDCT), a lossy audio compression algorithm. It is a modification of the discrete cosine transform (DCT) algorithm, which was proposed by Nasir Ahmed in 1972 for image compression. The DCT was adapted into the MDCT by J.P. Princen, A.W. Johnson and Alan B. Bradley at the University of Surrey in 1987.
Dolby Laboratories adapted the MDCT algorithm along with perceptual coding principles to develop the AC-3 audio format for cinema. The AC-3 format was released as the Dolby Digital standard in February 1991. Dolby Digital was the earliest MDCT-based audio compression standard released, and was followed by others for home and portable usage, such as Sony's ATRAC (1992), the MP3 standard (1993) and AAC (1997).

entries.title: Disneyland Paris opens
entries.subtitle: Disney's first European resort welcomes visitors
entries.summary: Euro Disneyland opened east of Paris in April 1992 as Disney's first European resort. A theme park, hotels and an entertainment district formed a destination that would later take the name Disneyland Paris.
body: Euro Disneyland opened to the public on 12 April 1992 at Marne-la-Vallée, east of Paris, after a weekend of previews and celebrations. Disney's first European resort combined one theme park with hotels and the Festival Disney entertainment district. An agreement signed with the French authorities in 1987 established the framework for the project, and construction began in 1988. The destination later became known as Disneyland Paris; a second theme park opened in 2002 under the name Walt Disney Studios Park.

entries.title: Jurassic Park
entries.summary: Jurassic Park turns a wildlife park filled with recreated dinosaurs into a survival crisis when its safeguards fail. Steven Spielberg's adaptation follows visiting experts and children whose fascination with the animals gives way to the need to escape them.
body: Steven Spielberg's Jurassic Park opened in US cinemas on 11 June 1993, adapting Michael Crichton's novel about a wildlife park populated by recreated dinosaurs. When power and security fail on Isla Nublar, visiting experts and children must escape the animals. Sam Neill, Laura Dern and Jeff Goldblum play members of the group confronted with the consequences of John Hammond's project. Crichton worked on the screenplay before David Koepp wrote the final draft, reducing exposition and changing characters. Filming took place in California and Hawaii in 1992, with post-production continuing while Spielberg worked on Schindler's List in Poland.
story_headings: A dinosaur park loses its safeguards
